query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. For tests (6) and (10): what does the literature report on (a) saturated-salt humidity chambers (Greenspan 1977; ISO 12571; OIML): accuracy, temperature sensitivity, equilibration time after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, sample size and layer thickness for gravimetric sorption, agreement with dynamic vapour sorption, and humidity effects on the flow of NaCl (deliquescence near 75 % RH), metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V) and pharmaceutical powders, including caking; (b) Faraday-cup measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio of powders after feeding, conveying or sieving: cup and shield design, electrometers versus home-built charge amplifiers (op-amp choice, feedback capacitor, leakage, guarding), collection efficiency for fines, typical charge-to-mass ratios for salts, metal powders and organic powders after contact with polymers (PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon) and steel, and their humidity dependence.
task_summary: Literature Review Of Saturated Salt Humidity Chambers And Faraday Cup Powder Charge Measurements

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:

Abstract:
An evaluated compilation of equilibrium relative humidities in air versus temperature from pure phase to approximately 105 pascal (1 atm) in pressure is presented for 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions. The relative humidities of the solutions range from about 3 to 98 percent. Using a data base from 21 separate investigations comprising 1106 individual measurements, fits were made by the method of least squares to regular polynomial equations with two through four coefficients. Equations and tables are presented along with the estimated uncertainties in the correlated results.

Abstract:
This paper is the second of two that examines between the hygroscopic behavior of sea salt aerosol proxies and the atmospheric corrosion of mild steel contaminated with them. In this work, artificial seawater (ASW) and MgCl2 were examined. The wetting and drying behavior of ASW was characterized by impedance measurements across an interdigitated electrode sensor. Steel coupons loaded with ASW and MgCl2 microparticles were subjected to isohumidity exposures for up to 30 days. The resulting damage was quantified by optical profilometry. The corrosion chemistry that developed was identified using EDS and Raman spectroscopy. Together, the results bring into question whether sea salt-contaminated surfaces ever dry in ambient outdoor environments. Sustained corrosion was detectable down to 11% RH for MgCl2 and 23% RH for ASW, with significant admittance of ASW deposits at <2% RH after 24 h, likely due to fluid trapping under a solid salt crust. Trends in corrosion loss versus RH were not directly reflective of the major liquid-solid phase transitions observed or predicted for ASW or MgCl2 alone. In light of this, common time of wetness determination methods are contended to be fundamentally flawed as quantitative indicators of electrolyte presence and the potential for significant corrosion. © The Author(s) 2014. Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and direct laser deposition (DLD) are the two main processes currently used in the additive manufacturing (AM) of metals. For both methods, metal powders are used as feedstock, and they must present specific physical and chemical properties to ensure optimal processing and reliable and reproducible printing results. Particle morphology, size distribution, and flowability, among other factors, depend on the powder production process and directly influence the processing parameters and physical characteristics of the parts built by AM. This systematic review presents different concepts involving L-PBF and DLD manufacturing and the application of metal powders. The methods used to produce and characterize metal powders and the modification techniques to improve their processability by AM are detailed and discussed. Environmental and health risks are also presented, and safety measures that must be considered while handling metal powders. Some key topics requiring attention for further development are highlighted. Graphical abstract

Abstract:
The most widely used metal additive manufacturing processes utilize powder that is spread or fed onto a building platform. Although there are reviews of the literature on some aspects of the powder, many aspects have been un-der-reviewed or unreviewed. The present work is a review of the literature on these aspects. Articles published in the open literature through the end of February 2022 were collected by consulting highly regarded relevant biblio-graphic databases, such as Google Scholar and Science Direct. The aspects reviewed were emerging methods of powder production, methods used to improve the quality of a powder after production by a well-established method, influence of variables of well-established powder production methods on powder properties, influence of powder production method on powder properties, and influence of powder reuse on properties of powders of a wide collection of alloys. One key finding was that with regard to powder reuse, the only consistent finding is that it leads to increase in the oxygen content of the powder. Another key finding was that the literature on the aspects of the literature reviewed herein contains many shortcomings and gaps, which suggest potential areas for future research, such as techniques for optimization of process variables for a given combination of metal powder and powder production method and development of methods for production of powders of new/emerging metallic materials.

Abstract:
In powder bed fusion additive manufacturing, the powder feedstock quality is of paramount importance; as the process relies on thin layers of powder being spread and selectively melted to manufacture 3D metallic components. Conventional powder quality assessments for additive manufacturing are limited to particle morphology, particle size distribution, apparent density and flowability. However, recent studies are highlighting that these techniques may not be the most appropriate. The problem is exacerbated when studying aluminium powders as their complex cohesive behaviors dictate their flowability. The current study compares the properties of three different AlSi7Mg powders, and aims to obtain insights about the minimum required properties for acceptable powder feedstock. In addition to conventional powder characterization assessments, the powder spread density, moisture sorption, surface energy, work of cohesion, and powder rheology, were studied. This work has shown that the presence of fine particles intensifies the pick-up of moisture increasing the total particle surface energy as well as the inter-particle cohesion. This effect hinders powder flow and hence, the spreading of uniform layers needed for optimum printing. This result suggest that by manipulating particle distribution, size and morphology, challenging powder feedstock such as Al, can be optimized for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
Metal powder-based additive manufacturing (AM) relies on consistently successful processing of feedstock powder, necessitating through-process predictability in powder properties and behavior. However, routine powder handling and storage may degrade powder performance by influencing flowability and moisture content through exposure to ambient conditions. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of repeated environmental exposure on the flowability and moisture content of Al 5056 and Ta powders for AM applications. Using Carney Funnel flow tests, thermogravimetric analysis, and particle size/shape analysis, powder characterization helped elucidate powder property and behavioral changes with exposure. Results indicated inconsistent flowability and moisture content changes for both material types when exposure conditions were altered. Correlational statistics highlighted the most influential particle characteristics on powder behavior after exposure; particle morphology was most impactful for the semi-spherical Al 5056, whereas moisture content and particle size were most significant for the angular Ta. While exposure to laboratory conditions minimally changed powder performance in this study, caution is advised when handling and storing powders in more “extreme” environments. Powder users are urged to implement quality controls alongside powder characterization to pinpoint how specific powders should be treated, handled, and stored in a given environment for successful processing in AM.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) has the advantages of high resolution and geometric freedom but can be susceptible to process failures and defects caused by inappropriate process parameters and powder conditions. This study aims to reveal and quantify the moisture effect on the qualities and properties of as-built parts with various process parameters. The results showed that the density was decreased by 7.86% with humid powder (60.0% relative humidity (RH)) compared to dry powder (3.4%RH). Expectedly, the observed low density led to the property degradation in the hardness, yield strength (YS), and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of the humid powder by 11.7, 15.02, and 21.25%, respectively, compared to that of dry powder (3.4%RH). Interestingly, the elongation at break of the parts fabricated with humid powder (60.0%RH) was increased by 2.82%, while their YS and UTS were decreased significantly. It seems that the water molecules on the powder surface hindered the reaction between the N2 shielding gas and melted powder, which resulted in the reduction in the austenite (γ) phase by up to 4.05 wt.%. This could be mainly responsible for the decrease in both the YS and UTS of the humid powder by approximately 100 and 150 MPa, respectively. This study demonstrates that the moisture of the metal powder used for LPBF should be carefully controlled to ensure desirable as-built qualities and properties.

Abstract:
Both producers and users of divided solids regularly face the problem of caking after periods of storage and/or transport. Particle agglomeration depends not only on powder water content, temperature and applied pressure, but also on the interactions between the solid substance and water molecules present in the atmosphere, i.e. on relative humidity (RH) at which the product is stored. Ambient humidity plays an important role in most events leading to caking: capillary condensation of water at contact points between particles, subsequent dissolution of a solid and formation of a saturated solution eventually followed by precipitation of the solid during the evaporation of water. Here, we focus on the kinetics of dissolution followed by evapo-recrystallization of a hygroscopic sodium chloride powder under controlled temperature and RH, with the aim of anticipating caking by predicting rates of water uptake and loss under industrial conditions. Precise measurements of water uptake show that the rate of dissolution is proportional to the difference between the imposed RH and deliquescence RH, and follows a model based on the kinetic theory of gases. Evaporation seems to be governed by more complex phenomena related to the mechanism of crystal growth from a supersaturated salt solution.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Étude multi-échelles du phénomène de mottage des poudres du lactose : de la physico-chimie des matériaux aux applications industrielles</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Cette thèse porte sur le problème fondamental du mottage des poudres suite aux mécanismes de transition de phase. Le projet vise à étudier l'impact des facteurs intrinsèques (structure moléculaire des matériaux, propriétés physiques et/ou physicochimiques, etc.) ou des facteurs environnementaux (conditions de stockage ou paramètres de procédé) sur la stabilité de la structure des poudres. Plus précisément, notre étude a mis en évidence le rôle prépondérant du phénomène de cristallisation et des transitions entre les différents polymorphes du lactose. L'accent a été mis sur le rôle des phénomènes de cristallisation et de la transition de phase dans l'apparition du mottage des poudres de lactose. Deux cas ont particulièrement retenu notre attention: (1) des poudres de lactose monohydrate contenant une fraction de particules amorphes et (2) des échantillons de poudre anhydre composés des anomères α et β du lactose. Dans les deux cas, le mottage a été induite par l'exposition des échantillons à l'air humide, soit dans un dispositif de sorption dynamique de vapeur (SPS), soit par des tests accélérés utilisant deux appareils conçus et réalisés dans notre laboratoire (CLAIR & OLAF). Nos résultats ont montré que, dans les deux cas, la principale cause de prise en masse était la formation de lactose monohydrate, qui est la forme la plus stable parmi tous les polymorphes de lactose. Cependant, les mécanismes élémentaires, les étapes limites et la cinétique du processus de transformation étaient différents dans chaque cas. Les paramètres les plus déterminants étaient l’humidité relative et la température alors que la pression n’a pas eu d’effet significatif. La résistance mécanique des échantillons mottés était étroitement liée au taux et à la cinétique de cristallisation. Enfin, des simulations numériques basées sur la méthode des éléments discrets (DEM) de la résistance mécanique des échantillons mottés ont été réalisées. Le modèle permet de décrire le comportement des échantillons mottés soumis à des contraintes mécaniques de compression ou de traction.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Electrostatic signals in pneumatic conveying depend on solids mass flow rate, air velocity, particle distribution and material, complicating direct estimation. This study classified five nominal solids mass flow rates (0.1–10 g/s) for wheat flour and ground coffee at four air velocities (15–30 m/s) using six ring electrodes and seven arc segments with guarded electrometer-grade front ends. From 1 s blocks, 29 time-, frequency- and time–frequency-domain features per channel were extracted. The Common Vector Approach (CVA), support vector machines (SVMs), multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), random forests (RFs) and feature-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were compared with an end-to-end CNN on raw signals. With one feeding cycle per record held out, the best balanced accuracies were 86.9% (flour) and 89.6% (coffee), and 97.8–100% of predictions were within one class. RF regression yielded typical error factors of 1.34 (flour) and 1.31 (coffee). Depending on the classifier, balanced accuracy declined to 47–70% for unseen air velocities and 26–59% across materials; a no-flow control suggested possible contributions from record-specific offsets to the accuracy. These findings restrict the reported performance to the tested conditions and support velocity-range coverage, material-specific calibration and recording-order controls.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Triboelectrification is the spontaneous charging of two bodies when released from contact. Even though its manifestation is commonplace, in for instance triboelectric nanogenerators, scientists find the tribocharging mechanism a mystery. The primary aim of this mini-review is to provide an overview of different tribocharging concepts that have been applied to study and realize the formation of ordered stable structures using different objects on various length scales. Relevance spans from materials to planet formations. Especially, dry assembly methods of particles of different shapes based on tribocharging to obtain crystal structures or monolayers are considered. In addition, the current technology employed to examine tribocharging in (semi)dry environments is discussed as well as the relevant forces playing a role in the assembly process. In brief, this mini-review is expected to provide a better understanding of tribocharging in assembling objects on the nano- and micrometer scales.

Abstract:
Contact electrification and triboelectric charging are areas of intense research. Despite their low ability to accept or donate electrons, polymer insulator based triboelectric nanogenerators have emerged as highly efficient mechanical‐to‐electrical conversion devices. Here, it is reviewed the structure–property–performance of polymer insulators in triboelectric nanogenerators and focus on tools that can be used to directly enhance charge generation, via altering a polymer's mechanical, thermal, chemical, and topographical properties. In addition to the discussion of these fundamental properties, the use of additives to locally manipulate the polymer surface structure is discussed. The link between each property and the underlying charging mechanism is discussed, in the context of both increasing surface charge and predicting the polarity of surface charge, and pathways to engineer triboelectric charging are highlighted. Key questions facing the field surrounding data reporting, the role of water, and synergy between mass, electron, and ion transfer mechanisms are highlighted with aspirational goals of a holistic model for triboelectric charging proposed.

Abstract:
Linear polyamides, known as nylons, are a class of synthetic polymers with a wide range of applications due to their outstanding properties, such as chemical and thermal resistance or mechanical strength. These polymers have been used in various fields: from common and domestic applications, such as socks and fishing nets, to industrial gears or water purification membranes. By their durability, flexibility and wear resistance, nylons are now being used in addictive manufacturing technology as a good material choice to produce sophisticated devices with precise and complex geometric shapes. Furthermore, the emergence of triboelectric nanogenerators and the development of biomaterials have highlighted the versatility and utility of these materials. Due to their ability to enhance triboelectric performance and the range of applications, nylons show a potential use as tribo-positive materials. Because of the easy control of their shape, they can be subsequently integrated into nanogenerators. The use of nylons has also extended into the field of biomaterials, where their biocompatibility, mechanical strength and versatility have paved the way for groundbreaking advances in medical devices as dental implants, catheters and non-absorbable surgical sutures. By means of 3D bioprinting, nylons have been used to develop scaffolds, joint implants and drug carriers with tailored properties for various biomedical applications. The present paper aims to collect evidence of these recently specific applications of nylons by reviewing the literature produced in recent decades, with a special focus on the newer technologies in the field of energy harvesting and biomedicine.

Abstract:
Triboelectric charging is present in numerous technologies and everyday processes, providing both problems and opportunities. Despite this, there is no generalised model for the amount of charge that will build up on surfaces in contact. Here, we develop a new model for the saturation charge on triboelectrically charged spherical insulators, accounting for both equalisation of surface potentials and electrical breakdown of the surrounding medium. Experiments are conducted under controlled temperature and humidity using two independent methods, measuring the saturation charge on polymer spheres contacting grounded stainless steel. The results verify our equalisation of surface potentials model which describes how saturation charge density increases for smaller particle sizes. Key triboelectric properties are calculated: The estimated saturation charge on a flat surface and the equalisation potential between different materials, which can be used to predict charge saturation and quantify a triboelectric series. The transition radius below which electrical breakdown will cause saturation of charge is also calculated theoretically. Limitations to the model are demonstrated experimentally. As particle size reduces, a point is reached at which the electrostatic adhesion of particles to the grounded charging surface prevents further charge build-up. Furthermore, it is found that the saturation charge for smaller particles in humid conditions is greatly reduced. These calculations, and the demonstrated procedure, can serve as a tool for the design of technologies and processes influenced by triboelectric charge build-up, including triboelectric nanogenerators and electrostatic mineral separators.

Abstract:
Contact electrification, or tribocharging, is pertinent to a broad range of industrial and natural processes involving dielectric materials. However, the basic mechanism by which charge is transferred between insulators is still unclear. Here, we use a simple apparatus that brings two macroscopic surfaces into repeated contact and measures the charge on the surfaces after each contact. We vary the temperature of the surfaces, and find that increasing temperature leads to a decrease in the magnitude of charge transfer. When paired with a Monte-Carlo simulation and TGA measurements, our results support a mechanism where adsorbed surface water is crucial for charge exchange. Our setup is easily extendable to a variety of industrially relevant materials.

Abstract:
We study the effect of humidity on the charge accumulation of polymer granulates shaken vertically in a stainless steel container. This setup allows us to control the humidity level from 5% to 100%RH while performing automated charge measurements in a Faraday cup directly connected to the shaking container. We find that samples of approximately 2000 polymer spheres become highly charged at low humidity levels (<30%RH), but acquire almost no charge for humidity levels above 80%RH. The transition between these two regimes does depend on the material, as does the sign of the charge. For the latter we find a correlation with the contact angle of the polymer with only very hydrophilic particles attaining positive charges. We show that this humidity dependence of tribo-charging can be used to control segregation in shaken binary mixtures.

Abstract:
The triboelectrostatic separation allows the sorting of granular polymers according to their contact charging characteristics. It consists in the appropriate triboelectric charging of particles, followed by their selective sorting in an electrostatic field. Exposed to a humid atmosphere, the polymer granules adsorb water moisture onto their surfaces, which modifies their charging characteristics, by improving the contact between surfaces. The present work was aimed at studying the effect of storage environmental conditions on the triboelectric charging of granular polymers in vibratory-type devices. Four granular different plastic wastes were placed in a climatic chamber and kept for 96 hours under controlled humidity, RH = 82% ± 4%, at 19 °C ± 1 °C. The measurement of the water content of the polymer granules pointed out an increase of at least 10% after 96 h of exposure to high relative humidity ambient conditions. The granules were successively charged by triboelectric effect in a vibratory device equipped with recipients in two different materials, at ambient conditions. The tribocharging efficiency was analyzed by measuring the electric charge of the granules with a Faraday pail connected to an electrometer. The thin water layer formed at the surface of the particle can explain their modified triboelectric behavior. The difference between the triboelectric charging behavior of “humid” and “normal” polymer granules depended also on the nature of the recipient of the tribocharging device.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Optimisation multi-variables et contrôle statistique des processus de charge triboélectrique des polymères</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">L'objectif principal de la thèse a été d'étudier le comportement triboélectrique des contacts glissants à sec entre matériaux polymères (ABS, PE, PP, PS et deux types de PVC), incluant la possibilité de contrôler et d'optimiser les résultats générés, en termes de charge électrique et d’usure. Un tribomètre linéaire a été conçu et construit, afin de permettre le réglage des principales variables de contrôle du processus de charge triboélectrique : force normale, vitesse de glissement, durée et course. Ce dispositif facilite la mesure de certaines grandeurs physiques caractérisant les conditions de frottement: les variations des forces normale et tangentielle, ainsi que le déplacement relatif entre les éprouvettes. De plus, la charge électrique générée et l’augmentation de la température à la surface du polymère ont été aussi été mesurées et mise en relation avec les propriétés tribologiques. Les expériences ont montré que le niveau et la distribution de la charge générée par le frottement sec dépendent de la force normale appliquée, du temps de frottement (le nombre de cycles), de la vitesse de glissement, des propriétés mécaniques des matériaux et de la rugosité ou de la texture des surfaces en contact. La décharge couronne peut être utilisée pour déposer une charge initiale sur les surfaces avant le glissement. La modélisation du processus de charge triboélectrique a été faite avec la méthodologie des plans d’expériences. Les résultats peuvent alors être utilisés pour prédire et optimiser la charge triboélectrique. Des cartes de contrôle peuvent assurer le monitoring du processus et la détection de variations non-maîtrisés de la charge générée par effet triboélectrique.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This paper presents a new study and analysis of the thermo-hygroscopic behavior of Arthrospira platensis using dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) system. Thermo-hygroscopic characterization is essential for optimizing the drying process and enhancing storage conditions. Therefore, the objective of this work was to investigate the thermo-hygroscopic properties of Arthrospira (Spirulina) platensis using a dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) system. This thermo-hygroscopic analysis focused on three fundamental parameters, namely: the desorption isotherms, the net isosteric heat of water desorption, and the moisture diffusivity. Desorption isotherms were measured at five different temperatures (25 °C, 40 °C, 50 °C, 60 °C and 80 °C) over a relative humidity range of 10–80%. The desorption isotherm data were fitted to five semi-empirical models: GAB, Oswin, Smith, Henderson, and Peleg. The results indicated that the GAB model provided the best fit for the experimental data. The net isosteric heat of desorption was determined using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation. It decreased from 21.3 to 4.29 KJ/mol as the equilibrium moisture content increased from 0.02 to 0.1 Kg/Kg (dry basis). Additionally, the moisture diffusivity of Arthrospira platensis was estimated based on Fick’s second law of diffusion and the desorption kinetics obtained from the DVS equipment. This parameter varied between 1.04 10−8 m2/s and 1.46 10−7 m2/s for average moisture contents ranging from 0.003 Kg/Kg to 0.191 Kg/Kg (dry basis). Furthermore, the activation energy for desorption was estimated to be approximately 33.7 KJ/mol.</jats:p>

The sensors remained over the solutions for 12 hours so that internal air humidity could reach equilibrium. The excerpt establishes Greenspan’s framework for assessing the accuracy of saturated-salt humidity fixed points, but it does not provide numerical equilibrium times or explicit dRH/dT values. The compilation covers 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions with relative humidities of approximately 3–98%, using 1,106 measurements from 21 investigations. Relative humidity was fitted as a function of temperature by least-squares regular polynomial equations, with the fitting procedure limited to polynomial order three and data between 0 and 104 °C. For uncertainty estimation, Greenspan calculated the standard deviation of the predicted relative humidity for each datum, then fitted those standard deviations versus temperature with a quadratic equation. At any selected temperature, three times the resulting predicted standard deviation was reported as the estimated uncertainty in RH, subject to exceptions discussed later in the paper. The excerpt notes that equilibration can be affected by humidity sources or sinks and by the initial equilibration process, but it gives no duration or criterion for reaching equilibrium. Likewise, determining temperature sensitivity would require differentiating the tabulated or fitted RH-versus-temperature equations, which are not included in these pages.

For relative-humidity sensor calibration measurements, the uncertainty budget included calibration uncertainty and temperature uncertainty. For isopiestic measurements, it included temperature differences, concentration determination, equilibrium uncertainty, and uncertainty in the reference-solution data. Abstract:
Faraday cups can measure velocity distribution functions of space plasmas and are frequent instruments on heliophysics missions. A new version of a Faraday cup instrument is in development for the Luna 26 mission and will be used for fast monitoring of the solar wind plasma parameters. The prototype of this instrument is exposed to dust impacts in a velocity range of 0.2–60 km s−1 using an electrostatic dust accelerator. The collected data are used to evaluate the sensitivity and detection efficiency of dust particles on two different surfaces. The results indicate that the sensitivity is sufficient for detection of the interplanetary dust as well as for the registration of the dust lifted from the lunar surface. A simple modification of the FC electronics would increase the detection efficiency by an order of magnitude.

<jats:p>The early stages of most particle accelerator chains produce sub-ns bunches with velocities in the range of 1% to 20% of the speed of light. Fast Faraday Cups (FFCs) are designed to measure the longitudinal charge distribution of these short bunches of free charges. Coaxial designs have been utilized at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research (GSI)’s linear accelerator UNILAC to characterize ion bunches with bunch lengths ranging from a few hundred ps to a few ns. The typical design goals are to avoid the pre-field of the charges and to suppress secondary electron emission (SEE) while preserving the capability of bunch-by-bunch measurements. This contribution presents a novel FFC design manufactured using additive manufacturing, e.g., laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), and compares it with a traditionally produced FFC. The article highlights the design process, RF characterization, and selected measurements with ion beam carried out at GSI.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The triboelectric charging of granular material is a long-standing and poorly understood phenomenon, with numerous scientific and industrial applications ranging from volcanic lightning to pharmaceutical production. The most widely utilised apparatus for the study of such charging is the Faraday cup, however, existing analysis of the resulting measurements is often simplistic and fails to distinguish charging due to particle-particle interactions from charging occurring through other mechanisms. Here, we outline a modular approach for interpreting these measurements, enabling triboelectric phenomena to be explored in greater detail. Our approach fits approximated charge distribution shapes to experimental Faraday cup traces. The fitting process uses measured size distributions in combination with simplified models of charge distribution and particle dynamics to predict the relative charging contributions. This modular approach allows scope for adaptation of each aspect to fine-tune the process to specific application cases, making the technique broadly generalisable to any insulating granular material. An example case of volcanic ash showed that samples from the Grímsvötn volcano charged with a greater proportion of particle-particle interactions than ash from Atitlán. Experimental validation is provided using sieved fractions of volcanic ash, where the broader size fractions were found to exhibit greater particle-particle charging. Non-particle-particle charging was also shown to scale with particle size as ∝ d-0.85±0.03p, roughly scaling with the particles' effective surface area.

Abstract:
The flowability of food powders is a critical determinant of their processing efficiency, product quality, and overall operational success. This review delves into the intricacies of powder flowability, elucidating the factors that govern it and exploring various methods for its evaluation and enhancement. Particle size and distribution, particle shape, surface properties, moisture content, and storage conditions stand as the key determinants of powder flowability. Finer powders, with their increased interparticle cohesive forces, tend to exhibit poorer flowability. Particle shape also plays a role, with irregular or elongated particles flowing less readily than spherical ones. Surface properties influence interparticle friction, thereby impacting flow behavior. Moisture content significantly affects flowability, as increased moisture can lead to liquid bridge formation, hindering powder movement. Storage temperature, on the other hand, generally enhances powder flow due to reduced interparticle cohesive forces at higher temperatures. This highlights the need to understand the factors influencing food powder flowability and to employ appropriate evaluation strategies for optimizing food powder processing efficiency, product quality, and overall production success.

The excerpt explains several ways humidity can reduce triboelectric charging of powders. Increased humidity may lower the dielectric strength of air, reducing the saturation charge on particles; smaller particles may show a larger reduction because they otherwise saturate at higher charge-density levels. Consequently, humidity can lower both the charging rate and the final saturation charge obtained during contact charging. Adsorbed water can form electrical double layers, with an immobile Stern layer and mobile Gouy-Chapman layer; interactions between these layers may also contribute to charge transfer through water bridges. The excerpt directly addresses humidity-related flow and spreadability degradation in AlSi10Mg and Ti6Al4V powders, although it does not provide detailed DVS methodology or specific storage-condition recommendations. Moisture is adsorbed through both physisorption and chemisorption. Physisorption is associated with capillary forces and liquid bridges between particles; for micrometer-scale particles, the capillary force is reported to be largely independent of relative humidity once moisture is entrapped, allowing agglomerations to persist. AlSi10Mg, whose particles are more irregular and rough, readily takes up moisture. Its moisture content can become six times the initial value after moisturizing, exhibits substantial measurement variability, and is difficult to remove by drying. Moisture-related agglomeration, combined with irregular morphology and a wider particle-size distribution, obstructs the applicator aperture and produces nonuniform powder layers, lines, particle-free regions, and potentially manufacturing defects such as porosity and dimensional inconsistencies. Ti6Al4V has spherical, homogeneous particles and shows very low moisture pickup in all tested states, indicating lower sorption susceptibility. Nevertheless, moisturizing still causes agglomeration, consistent with capillary-bridge behavior. Vacuum and air drying are mentioned as treatments, but the excerpt does not quantify their effectiveness for Ti6Al4V or give controlled humidity storage limits.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3'.

Marina Langlet, Frederic Nadaud, Mohammed Benali, Isabelle Pezron, Khashayar Saleh, Pierre Guigon, and Léa Metlas-Komunjer. Kinetics of dissolution and recrystallization of sodium chloride at controlled relative humidity. Kona Powder and Particle Journal, 29:168-179, Jan 2011. URL: https://doi.org/10.14356/kona.2011019, doi:10.14356/kona.2011019. This article has 56 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

At 25°C, sodium chloride has a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75%. Below this threshold, the crystalline phase is thermodynamically favored; at or above it, water uptake and formation of an aqueous salt solution become favorable. For powder flow and storage, increasing humidity can promote capillary condensation at particle contact points, creating liquid bridges. These bridges dissolve NaCl locally and can initiate particle agglomeration and caking. If environmental humidity or temperature subsequently changes and water evaporates, the saturated or supersaturated solution recrystallizes, producing solid bridges that generally bind particles more strongly than liquid bridges. The resulting cake strength depends on temperature, humidity, pressure, mass transfer, powder solubility, and the number of particle contact points. Kinetically, the study reports that NaCl dissolution under controlled conditions increases with the humidity driving force: the dissolution rate is proportional to the difference between imposed RH and the DRH. Dynamic Vapor Sorption measurements can track water uptake during deliquescence and water loss during recrystallization. In contrast, evaporation and recrystallization are not described by the same simple relationship; they appear to depend on more complex crystal-growth processes from a supersaturated salt solution. Small particles may dissolve before larger agglomerates, producing nonequilibrium behavior within a powder bed.

The excerpt identifies sodium chloride’s deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) as approximately 75–76% RH under the stated conditions. Above this threshold, water vapor uptake and capillary condensation produce liquid at crystal contacts, enabling NaCl dissolution; below the DRH, lowering water-vapor pressure promotes recrystallization. This provides the basis for understanding humidity-driven changes in powder flow: condensed liquid bridges connect particles and initiate caking, which can impair powder mobility and handling. Environmental scanning electron microscopy is used to observe wetting and drying, while dynamic vapor sorption measures mass uptake and its rate. The proposed kinetic model applies Knudsen gas-kinetic theory, relating the net water-molecule flux to the difference between imposed vapor pressure or water activity and the saturated-solution value. Experiments used millimeter-scale NaCl crystals at controlled temperature and humidity; at 2°C, changing water-vapor pressure between approximately 3 and 5 Torr produced conditions above or below the roughly 75% DRH. At 72% RH, liquid at crystal contacts was too small to observe microscopically, whereas at 83% RH a substantial condensed liquid volume and wetting of the crystal surfaces were visible. The resulting saturated solution and liquid bridges constitute the initial structural mechanism of caking.

The excerpt describes how NaCl powder responds as relative humidity approaches or exceeds its deliquescence relative humidity (DRH), which is relevant to behavior near 75% RH. Water uptake and loss are governed by the difference between imposed RH and DRH: closer to or above DRH, the rate of moisture uptake and dissolution increases, while below DRH evaporation and recrystallization occur. ESEM observations indicate that dissolution at high RH is relatively homogeneous, with individual crystals and aggregates taking up water simultaneously. The reported 25 °C data show strong RH dependence: after four days, 25.5% of NaCl dissolved at 80% RH, 57.3% at 85% RH, and 80.3% at 90% RH. Thus, a condition at 75% RH would be expected to produce substantially less dissolution than these measured conditions if it is below or only near the DRH, although the excerpt does not provide a direct 75% RH measurement. During drying below DRH, recrystallization proceeds through distinct stages: growth from partially dissolved aggregates and nucleation/growth from homogeneous solution formed by complete dissolution. These processes produce larger, more compact clusters and alter particle size and shape, providing the caking mechanism. The excerpt does not directly quantify powder-flow changes, but the observed aggregation and caking imply deterioration of flowability.

The excerpt compares the dynamic DVS method with the static saturated-salt/COST 90 method across MCC powder, pharmaceutical granules, and a PEBA membrane. Agreement is good for MCC and pharmaceutical granules across the measured water-activity range, apparently because internal diffusion is not sufficiently limiting. For MCC, diffusion was evaluated using a 500 µm-thick powder slab; the estimated apparent diffusion coefficients were about 1.7 × 10^-9 m²/s at relative humidity 0.8 and 4.4 × 10^-9 m²/s at 0.2. The authors suggest that coefficients above approximately 10^-9 m²/s do not cause significant disagreement between static and dynamic measurements. For pharmaceutical granules, modeled as spheres with radius 0.625 mm, agreement was also good. Their relatively large diameter compared with the crucible prevented preparation of a powder layer, so transfer limitations could occur only within individual particles. Equilibration was much faster with DVS: approximately 5 hours versus 7 days for saturated salts at the highest water activity. For PEBA, agreement was good below water activity 0.6 but deteriorated at higher activity, where internal diffusion increasingly controlled sorption. DVS required about 19 hours, whereas saturated salts required about 12 days at 90% relative humidity and still may not have reached thermodynamic equilibrium.

Consequently, charge-to-mass values are expected to vary substantially with equipment, material, operating conditions, and measurement procedure rather than having a single universal value. The excerpt identifies the Faraday pail or Faraday well as the standard method for measuring electrostatic charge, which can be combined with powder mass to determine charge-to-mass ratio. It also discusses triboelectric series qualitatively: a material charges positive relative to materials below it in the series, but the ordering and observed charge are specific to experimental conditions. The provided pages do not list positions for PLA, PTFE, nylon, or PETG, nor do they provide enough of Table 1 to infer those positions. Additional experimental data or a source containing a complete, condition-specific triboelectric series and operation-specific charge measurements is required.

## pqac-00000061

From text 'rorigdalgaard2016highaccuracycalibration pages 5-6'.

Inge Rörig-Dalgaard and Staffan Svensson. High accuracy calibration of a dynamic vapor sorption instrument and determination of the equilibrium humidities using single salts. The Review of scientific instruments, 87 5:054101, May 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4949513, doi:10.1063/1.4949513. This article has 14 citations.

The excerpt indicates that equilibration of a saturated salt-water lump requires controlled humidity changes and sufficient time. In the calibration procedure, the chamber was maintained at RH above the salt solution’s equilibrium RH for one hour to ensure that the entire lump reached equilibrium; the associated mass increase reflected water uptake and partial salt dissolution. The chamber RH then needed to be changed slowly enough for the salt and surrounding air to equilibrate, with the rate of RH change adjusted as necessary. Equilibrium was assessed by comparing absorption and desorption behavior: under satisfactory conditions, the fitted lines coincided at the equilibrium point, corresponding to zero mass change. If the salt-water mixture was too wet or too dry, the intersection shifted away from the zero-mass-change point, providing a diagnostic of inadequate preparation. The excerpt does not provide a specific equilibration time after opening a humidity chamber, quantify the effect of a mixing fan, describe re-equilibration after an external disturbance, or discuss air circulation in a desiccator. It does note that dry salt was stored in a dry-climate desiccator below 5% RH before preparation, and that approximately 25 mg of salt was used to promote rapid equilibration while retaining measurement accuracy.

L. B. Rockland. Saturated salt solutions for static control of relative humidity between 5° and 40° c. Analytical Chemistry, 32:1375-1376, Sep 1960. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/ac60166a055, doi:10.1021/ac60166a055. This article has 1105 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt is directly relevant to equilibration in saturated-salt humidity chambers because it introduces a table specifically titled “Effect of Mechanical Convection on Equilibration Rates of Electric Hygrometer with Atmosphere over Saturated Salt Solutions.” The table is intended to report the time, in minutes, required for relative-humidity increments under different saturated salts, including lithium chloride and sodium bromide, with and without mechanical convection. This indicates that air circulation or a mixing fan was experimentally evaluated as a factor affecting the speed at which the chamber atmosphere reaches equilibrium. However, the supplied excerpt cuts off before the numerical table entries and does not provide the actual equilibration times, fan speeds, or a quantitative comparison between mixed and still air. It also does not state how long a chamber requires to re-equilibrate after opening or other disturbance, nor does it give a specific air-circulation procedure for a desiccator. The introductory text emphasizes that saturated salt solutions are commonly used to establish controlled relative humidities and warns that even small temperature changes can significantly alter equilibrium relative humidity. Therefore, the excerpt supports the relevance of mechanical convection and temperature stability but cannot establish precise equilibration or re-equilibration times.

## pqac-00000063

From text 'imre1964themeasurementof pages 1-4'.

L Imre. The measurement of equilibrium relative humidity part i. Unknown journal, 1964.

The excerpt provides general guidance on equilibration in humidity chambers but does not give a specific equilibration time after opening, quantify the effect of a mixing fan, or describe re-equilibration after a disturbance. It states that measurements are normally performed in a generally closed, thermostatically controlled chamber, using a sulfuric-acid or salt solution to establish the desired vapor tension. Equilibrium is identified operationally when consecutive sample-weight measurements remain constant, after which the chamber’s equilibrium relative humidity is determined. The system reaching equilibrium is not simply the salt solution and air: it includes the sample, air, and absorbent as a multicomponent system. During desorption, moisture transfers from the sample to the absorbent through the ambient air, so the absorbent concentration changes as it takes up water. The excerpt also notes that, for a fixed-size sample, the time required to reach practically constant weight generally increases as the chamber’s vapor tension increases. These principles imply that opening the chamber or otherwise disturbing it would require waiting until the intended temperature and vapor-tension conditions are restored and verified, but the excerpt supplies no numerical waiting period or direct evidence about forced air circulation, fan operation, or desiccator air mixing.

From text 'rorigdalgaard2016highaccuracycalibration pages 6-8'.

Inge Rörig-Dalgaard and Staffan Svensson. High accuracy calibration of a dynamic vapor sorption instrument and determination of the equilibrium humidities using single salts. The Review of scientific instruments, 87 5:054101, May 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4949513, doi:10.1063/1.4949513. This article has 14 citations.

The excerpt does not directly study saturated-salt humidity chambers after opening, mixing-fan effects, or re-equilibration in a desiccator. It does provide related information from dynamic vapor sorption calibration tests. Longer test durations reduce the influence of heat generated by dissolution on the chamber microclimate because the instrument maintains constant air flow; this improves the representativeness of the measured equilibrium relative humidity. The authors used a controlled sequence beginning with evaporation until RH fell below the salt solution’s equilibrium RH, followed by absorption, rather than relying on a single equilibration direction. Their optimized durations varied substantially by salt: LiCl and KNO3 required about 20 h, MgCl2 about 6 h, and Mg(NO3)2 and NaCl about 10 h, with an initial hour at the highest RH. The table reports RH rates and narrow operating intervals around the equilibrium RH, indicating that equilibration requirements depend strongly on salt properties. The text also states that approximately 3% water relative to solid salt mass was needed for each additional hour of sequence duration. These findings suggest that air circulation and extended waiting can help restore stable RH after a disturbance, but the excerpt gives no direct time constant or protocol for opening a chamber or using a mixing fan.

From text 'rorigdalgaard2016highaccuracycalibration pages 3-4'.

Inge Rörig-Dalgaard and Staffan Svensson. High accuracy calibration of a dynamic vapor sorption instrument and determination of the equilibrium humidities using single salts. The Review of scientific instruments, 87 5:054101, May 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4949513, doi:10.1063/1.4949513. This article has 14 citations.

The excerpt is relevant to equilibration and re-equilibration after a saturated-salt humidity chamber is opened or otherwise disturbed, but it does not provide a specific equilibration time, fan-speed recommendation, or direct comparison of stirred versus unstirred chambers. It emphasizes that salt–water systems may require relatively long periods to reach equilibrium because dissolution kinetics, ion diffusion, and moisture exchange with the surrounding environment all contribute. The time required for deliquescence increases as the imposed relative humidity approaches the salt solution’s equilibrium relative humidity, indicating especially slow adjustment near equilibrium. The authors describe equilibrium operationally through the absence of continuing sample-mass change: below the deliquescence point, water evaporates; above it, the mixture absorbs water; and equilibrium is reached when dm/dt equals zero. These observations support monitoring humidity and/or mass until the system stabilizes after exposure to ambient air. The passage does not discuss air circulation in a desiccator or the specific effect of a mixing fan, although environmental moisture exchange is identified as an important factor. It also warns that inadequate moisture control can produce RH calibration uncertainty as large as ±2.5%.

From text 'cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51'.

RD Cruise. Triboelectric charging of insulating materials-understanding, manipulation and application to lunar in-situ resource utilisation. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt describes the principles directly relevant to an ADA4530-1 electrometer charge amplifier used with a Faraday cup, although it does not name the ADA4530-1 or provide a specific circuit design. The Faraday cup’s inner conducting cup connects to the coulombmeter’s inverting input, while the non-inverting input is grounded. A known feedback capacitor, C_F, is placed between the amplifier output and inverting input. Charge is obtained by integrating the input current: q = ∫I_in dt = C_F V_F, so the capacitor value determines the charge-to-voltage conversion and must be selected with the expected charge range and noise in mind. The excerpt emphasizes that input bias current causes measurement drift, with temperature and relative humidity potentially worsening the effect by changing component and insulator resistance. Triboelectric currents can also arise from mechanical friction, including twisting the BNC cable, and can be significant in very low-current measurements. For shielding and leakage/noise reduction, the recommended Faraday cup uses an inner measurement cup inside a larger grounded outer conducting cup, separated by insulation; the outer cup acts as a Faraday cage. The passage does not explicitly discuss driven guarding, guard-ring layout, insulation resistance, or ADA4530-1-specific leakage specifications, so those design details must be obtained from the op-amp datasheet and application guidance.

## pqac-00000071

From text 'cruise2023triboelectricchargingofa pages 47-51'.

RD Cruise. Triboelectric charging of insulating materials-understanding, manipulation and application to lunar in-situ resource utilisation. Unknown journal, 2023.

The excerpt describes the core charge-amplifier principles relevant to an ADA4530-1 electrometer design. A Faraday cup uses an inner conducting cup connected to the coulombmeter and a larger grounded outer cup, with insulation between them. The outer cup functions as a Faraday cage and provides electromagnetic shielding. When a charged particle enters the inner cup, an equal and opposite induced charge is supplied through the amplifier input, producing an induced current. An inverting integrating amplifier uses a known feedback capacitor, C_F, between its output and inverting input; the measured feedback voltage gives charge through q = ∫I_in dt = C_F V_F. The excerpt emphasizes that the observed charge signal can drift because of amplifier input bias current and triboelectric currents. Input bias is an imbalance between amplifier input currents and may worsen with temperature and relative humidity. Triboelectric current can arise from mechanical friction in the cabling, such as twisting a BNC cable and rubbing its center conductor against the insulating shield. These effects are important leakage/noise sources when measuring small Faraday-cup charges. The passage does not specifically discuss the ADA4530-1, driven guarding, guard-ring implementation, or detailed leakage-current calculations.
