{"answer": "## Literature Review for Tests (6) and (10): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Faraday-Cup Charge-to-Mass Ratio Measurement

---

### Part (a): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Humidity Effects on Powder Flow

#### 1. Accuracy of Saturated-Salt Humidity Fixed Points

The definitive reference for saturated-salt humidity fixed points is Greenspan (1977), who compiled equilibrium relative humidity (RH) data for 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions using 1,106 measurements from 21 investigations, fitted as polynomial functions of temperature (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000066). Uncertainties were assigned as three times the standard deviation of the predicted values, with individual datum uncertainties propagated through a root-sum-square combination of contributions from temperature, pressure, equilibrium attainment, and sensor calibration (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004). At 25 °C, the reported uncertainties for salts commonly used in humidity chambers are: LiCl 11.3 ± 0.3% RH; MgCl₂ 32.8 ± 0.2% RH; Mg(NO₃)₂ 52.9 ± 0.2% RH; NaCl 75.3 ± 0.2% RH; KCl 84.3 ± 0.3% RH; KNO₃ 93.6 ± 0.6% RH; and K₂SO₄ 97.3 ± 0.5% RH (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000069). Lu and Chen (2007) used these Greenspan values to calibrate humidity sensors with vessels maintained at 25 ± 0.2 °C and 12-hour equilibration periods, reporting that the dominant contribution to combined uncertainty was the predicted calibration uncertainty of the sensor itself rather than the salt reference (pqac-00000000).

The following table summarizes the Greenspan fixed points for the specific salts proposed in the user's setup:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

#### 2. Temperature Sensitivity

The temperature coefficient dRH/dT varies considerably among salts. From the polynomial coefficients in Greenspan's Table 1 (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067), NaCl has a relatively small temperature sensitivity of approximately −0.07% RH/°C near 25 °C, whereas Mg(NO₃)₂ is approximately −0.30% RH/°C—meaning that a ±1 °C temperature excursion shifts the nominal RH by ∓0.3 percentage points for Mg(NO₃)₂ but only ∓0.07 for NaCl. MgCl₂ has an even flatter coefficient (approximately −0.06% RH/°C), making it one of the most temperature-insensitive fixed points (pqac-00000069). Rockland (1960) emphasized the desirability of salts with low temperature coefficients and warned that even small temperature variations can cause significant changes in equilibrium RH (pqac-00000062). Rörig-Dalgaard and Svensson (2016) cautioned that heat of solution during salt dissolution or crystallization can locally change temperature and thus calibration RH, noting that inadequate moisture control can produce calibration uncertainty as large as ±2.5% RH (pqac-00000065).

#### 3. Equilibration Time and Effect of Mixing Fans

Equilibration time depends strongly on the salt, chamber volume, sample loading, and air circulation. In dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) calibration, salt-specific test durations ranged from approximately 6 hours for MgCl₂ to 20 hours for LiCl and KNO₃, with NaCl and Mg(NO₃)₂ requiring approximately 10 hours (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000064). For static desiccator-type chambers, equilibration can require days to weeks, particularly at high RH (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000063). Rockland (1960) explicitly evaluated the effect of mechanical convection (a mixing fan) on equilibration rates and reported that fans decreased the time to achieve equilibration by 10 to 50 times compared to still-air conditions (pqac-00000062). This strongly supports including a small circulating fan within each humidity chamber to accelerate recovery after opening.

#### 4. Sample Size and Layer Thickness for Gravimetric Sorption

Traditional saturated-salt-solution (SSS) gravimetric sorption methods typically require large samples of 10–100 g, with equilibration periods of days to weeks (pqac-00000054). Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) instruments use much smaller samples, typically 20–100 mg, with equilibration at each RH step achievable in hours rather than days (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000026). For the proposed few-gram setup using the doser, intermediate between these extremes, the key consideration is ensuring that the powder layer is thin enough for vapor to penetrate the bed rapidly. Arlabosse et al. (2003) found that for materials with apparent diffusion coefficients above approximately 10⁻⁹ m²/s, good agreement between static and dynamic methods was obtained; a 500 µm powder slab of microcrystalline cellulose gave diffusion coefficients of 1.7–4.4 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s and produced consistent results (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

#### 5. Agreement Between DVS and Saturated-Salt Methods

Good agreement between DVS and SSS methods has been reported for several powder materials, particularly at low to intermediate RH. For microcrystalline cellulose, pharmaceutical granules, and barley straw, DVS and SSS isotherms generally agreed well (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000051). Disagreement can arise at high water activity (above ~0.6–0.8) where slow internal diffusion limits the sample's ability to reach thermodynamic equilibrium within DVS step times (pqac-00000047). The DVS mass-stability criterion is typically 100 times less stringent than the SSS criterion, which partly accounts for DVS being faster but potentially less accurate at high RH (pqac-00000049). For materials with dense or laminated structures, the methods may disagree because DVS results become dependent on sorption rate rather than thermodynamic equilibrium (pqac-00000053).

#### 6. Humidity Effects on NaCl (Deliquescence Near 75% RH)

Sodium chloride has a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75–76% at 25 °C (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042). Below this threshold, the crystalline phase is thermodynamically stable; at or above DRH, water uptake initiates dissolution and formation of a saturated aqueous solution. The dissolution rate is proportional to the difference between imposed RH and DRH (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). At 80% RH, approximately 25.5% of NaCl dissolves after four days; at 85% RH, 57.3%; and at 90% RH, 80.3% (pqac-00000041). Operating at exactly 75% RH places NaCl dangerously close to its DRH: small temperature or humidity fluctuations can trigger partial dissolution, formation of liquid bridges at particle contacts, and subsequent recrystallization upon drying, producing solid bridges and irreversible caking (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042). Dense NaCl powder aggregates can take days or weeks to deliquesce completely because vapor transport is restricted within the powder bed (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). This suggests that the NaCl chamber should ideally be omitted for conditioning NaCl powder itself, as the equilibrium RH of saturated NaCl coincides with NaCl's own DRH.

#### 7. Humidity Effects on Metal AM Powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V)

Among metal AM powders, AlSi10Mg is the most susceptible to moisture uptake, with moisture content increasing up to six times the initial value after conditioning at 50 °C and 80% RH for 72 hours (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028). The irregular and rough particle morphology of AlSi10Mg promotes moisture adsorption through both physisorption and chemisorption, leading to thicker oxide layers, agglomeration via capillary bridges, and severely degraded spreadability (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024). DVS measurements on similar AlSi7Mg powders showed that fine particles contribute most to moisture sorption due to their greater specific surface area; removing fines by sieving substantially reduced vapor uptake (pqac-00000027). Ti-6Al-4V, with its spherical and homogeneous particle morphology, shows very low moisture pickup in all tested states, indicating much lower sorption susceptibility (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). Nevertheless, even Ti-6Al-4V can form moisture-mediated agglomerates via capillary bridges (pqac-00000023). Drying practices in the literature typically use 80–190 °C, with vacuum drying at 85 °C for 12 hours producing effective moisture removal (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000024).

#### 8. Humidity Effects on Pharmaceutical Powders and Caking

Pharmaceutical powders such as lactose are particularly susceptible to humidity-induced caking. Amorphous fractions within otherwise crystalline powders are hygroscopic and can crystallize when exposed to humid air, releasing water and forming solid bridges (pqac-00000046). The caking mechanism involves condensation, dissolution, and recrystallization at particle contacts, driven by the difference between ambient RH and the material's critical RH or DRH (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046). Caking strength correlates with the rate and extent of crystallization, and repeated humidity cycling generally worsens the effect. Storage of hygroscopic powders over saturated solutions of MgCl₂, NaBr, NaCl, and KCl has been used to study caking at controlled RH levels (pqac-00000042).

---

### Part (b): Faraday-Cup Measurement of Powder Charge-to-Mass Ratio

#### 1. Cup and Shield Design

The standard Faraday cup for powder charge measurement consists of a conducting inner measurement cup surrounded by a larger grounded conducting outer cup, with an electrically insulating material (typically Teflon) separating them (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The outer cup functions as a Faraday cage, reducing electromagnetic background noise (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013). A BNC or coaxial cable connects the assembly to the measurement electronics: the cable shield connects to the grounded outer cup, while the center conductor connects to the inner cup (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). Very high insulation between the inner and outer cups is required to minimize charge decay (pqac-00000008). Sowinski (2012) described concentric cylindrical copper vessels with inner dimensions of 0.15 m diameter × 0.25 m height and outer dimensions of 0.20 m diameter × 0.33 m height, isolated by Teflon bolts and connected to a Keithley 6514 electrometer (pqac-00000009). For the proposed bench-top setup with a 3 mm doser outlet, a smaller aluminium cup inside a grounded can is appropriate.

#### 2. Collection Efficiency for Fines

Collection efficiency for fine particles is a recognized challenge. Sowinski (2012) used a reusable filter bag with only 26–30% capture efficiency for 1 µm particulates (pqac-00000009). Sun et al. (2019) designed a mini-Faraday cup with an internal metal disc filter specifically to achieve high collection efficiency for charged ultrafine particles in the 50–300 nm range, with measured current showing good linearity with particle concentration (pqac-00000014). For the proposed setup collecting auger-dosed powder, ensuring that all fine particles land in the cup rather than being lost to air currents or electrostatic adhesion to walls is important; a deep cup geometry and controlled drop height help maximize collection.

#### 3. Electrometers Versus Home-Built Charge Amplifiers

Commercial electrometers (e.g., Keithley 6514) provide turnkey charge/current measurement with proven specifications but at high cost (pqac-00000009). For a home-built charge amplifier, the critical component is an electrometer-grade CMOS op-amp with ultra-low input bias current (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). Two leading candidates are:

- **LMP7721** (Texas Instruments): 3 fA typical input bias current, 17 MHz gain-bandwidth product, rail-to-rail output. Its ultra-low bias current makes it suitable for sub-picoampere transimpedance and charge-integrator circuits (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).
- **ADA4530-1** (Analog Devices): ~20 fA typical input bias current, designed specifically for electrometer applications with on-chip guarding (pqac-00000036).

The charge amplifier operates as an integrator: a known feedback capacitor C_F between the output and inverting input converts input charge to voltage according to q = C_F × V_F (pqac-00000070). The feedback capacitor value determines both sensitivity and dynamic range; smaller capacitors give higher sensitivity but saturate sooner. A parallel high-value resistor or periodic reset switch prevents drift from integrating bias current (pqac-00000037). Input capacitance (~11 pF for LMP7721) combined with PCB stray capacitance forms a pole with feedback components that can cause instability; a feedback capacitor may be needed for compensation, with the value determined experimentally (pqac-00000031).

#### 4. Leakage, Guarding, and Practical Implementation

At femtoampere current levels, leakage from PCB traces, connectors, and insulation dominates measurement error (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000074). Guarding is essential: a driven guard trace surrounds the high-impedance input and feedback nodes, maintained at approximately the same potential as the protected node, so that voltage differences across insulation are eliminated and leakage current is diverted into the low-impedance guard rather than the input (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000072). The guard should form a complete conductive enclosure including guard planes connected through vias, with an external ground plane or shield protecting it from noise and leakage (pqac-00000032). Triaxial cables extend guarding along cables to the Faraday cup (pqac-00000032). ---

### Part (a): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Humidity Effects on Powder Flow

#### 1. Accuracy of Saturated-Salt Humidity Fixed Points

The definitive reference for saturated-salt humidity fixed points is Greenspan (1977), who compiled equilibrium relative humidity (RH) data for 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions using 1,106 measurements from 21 investigations, fitted as polynomial functions of temperature (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000066). Uncertainties were assigned as three times the standard deviation of the predicted values, with individual datum uncertainties propagated through a root-sum-square combination of contributions from temperature, pressure, equilibrium attainment, and sensor calibration (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004). At 25 °C, the reported uncertainties for salts commonly used in humidity chambers are: LiCl 11.3 ± 0.3% RH; MgCl₂ 32.8 ± 0.2% RH; Mg(NO₃)₂ 52.9 ± 0.2% RH; NaCl 75.3 ± 0.2% RH; KCl 84.3 ± 0.3% RH; KNO₃ 93.6 ± 0.6% RH; and K₂SO₄ 97.3 ± 0.5% RH (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000069). Lu and Chen (2007) used these Greenspan values to calibrate humidity sensors with vessels maintained at 25 ± 0.2 °C and 12-hour equilibration periods, reporting that the dominant contribution to combined uncertainty was the predicted calibration uncertainty of the sensor itself rather than the salt reference (pqac-00000000).

The following table summarizes the Greenspan fixed points for the specific salts proposed in the user's setup:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

#### 2. Temperature Sensitivity

The temperature coefficient dRH/dT varies considerably among salts. From the polynomial coefficients in Greenspan's Table 1 (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067), NaCl has a relatively small temperature sensitivity of approximately −0.07% RH/°C near 25 °C, whereas Mg(NO₃)₂ is approximately −0.30% RH/°C—meaning that a ±1 °C temperature excursion shifts the nominal RH by ∓0.3 percentage points for Mg(NO₃)₂ but only ∓0.07 for NaCl. MgCl₂ has an even flatter coefficient (approximately −0.06% RH/°C), making it one of the most temperature-insensitive fixed points (pqac-00000069). Rockland (1960) emphasized the desirability of salts with low temperature coefficients and warned that even small temperature variations can cause significant changes in equilibrium RH (pqac-00000062). Rörig-Dalgaard and Svensson (2016) cautioned that heat of solution during salt dissolution or crystallization can locally change temperature and thus calibration RH, noting that inadequate moisture control can produce calibration uncertainty as large as ±2.5% RH (pqac-00000065).

#### 3. Equilibration Time and Effect of Mixing Fans

Equilibration time depends strongly on the salt, chamber volume, sample loading, and air circulation. In dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) calibration, salt-specific test durations ranged from approximately 6 hours for MgCl₂ to 20 hours for LiCl and KNO₃, with NaCl and Mg(NO₃)₂ requiring approximately 10 hours (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000064). For static desiccator-type chambers, equilibration can require days to weeks, particularly at high RH (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000063). Rockland (1960) explicitly evaluated the effect of mechanical convection (a mixing fan) on equilibration rates and reported that fans decreased the time to achieve equilibration by 10 to 50 times compared to still-air conditions (pqac-00000062). This strongly supports including a small circulating fan within each humidity chamber to accelerate recovery after opening.

#### 4. Sample Size and Layer Thickness for Gravimetric Sorption

Traditional saturated-salt-solution (SSS) gravimetric sorption methods typically require large samples of 10–100 g, with equilibration periods of days to weeks (pqac-00000054). Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) instruments use much smaller samples, typically 20–100 mg, with equilibration at each RH step achievable in hours rather than days (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000026). For the proposed few-gram setup using the doser, intermediate between these extremes, the key consideration is ensuring that the powder layer is thin enough for vapor to penetrate the bed rapidly. Arlabosse et al. (2003) found that for materials with apparent diffusion coefficients above approximately 10⁻⁹ m²/s, good agreement between static and dynamic methods was obtained; a 500 µm powder slab of microcrystalline cellulose gave diffusion coefficients of 1.7–4.4 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s and produced consistent results (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

#### 5. Agreement Between DVS and Saturated-Salt Methods

Good agreement between DVS and SSS methods has been reported for several powder materials, particularly at low to intermediate RH. For microcrystalline cellulose, pharmaceutical granules, and barley straw, DVS and SSS isotherms generally agreed well (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000051). Disagreement can arise at high water activity (above ~0.6–0.8) where slow internal diffusion limits the sample's ability to reach thermodynamic equilibrium within DVS step times (pqac-00000047). The DVS mass-stability criterion is typically 100 times less stringent than the SSS criterion, which partly accounts for DVS being faster but potentially less accurate at high RH (pqac-00000049). For materials with dense or laminated structures, the methods may disagree because DVS results become dependent on sorption rate rather than thermodynamic equilibrium (pqac-00000053).

#### 6. Humidity Effects on NaCl (Deliquescence Near 75% RH)

Sodium chloride has a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75–76% at 25 °C (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042). Below this threshold, the crystalline phase is thermodynamically stable; at or above DRH, water uptake initiates dissolution and formation of a saturated aqueous solution. The dissolution rate is proportional to the difference between imposed RH and DRH (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). At 80% RH, approximately 25.5% of NaCl dissolves after four days; at 85% RH, 57.3%; and at 90% RH, 80.3% (pqac-00000041). Operating at exactly 75% RH places NaCl dangerously close to its DRH: small temperature or humidity fluctuations can trigger partial dissolution, formation of liquid bridges at particle contacts, and subsequent recrystallization upon drying, producing solid bridges and irreversible caking (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042). Dense NaCl powder aggregates can take days or weeks to deliquesce completely because vapor transport is restricted within the powder bed (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). This suggests that the NaCl chamber should ideally be omitted for conditioning NaCl powder itself, as the equilibrium RH of saturated NaCl coincides with NaCl's own DRH.

Among metal AM powders, AlSi10Mg is the most susceptible to moisture uptake, with moisture content increasing up to six times the initial value after conditioning at 50 °C and 80% RH for 72 hours (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028). DVS measurements on similar AlSi7Mg powders showed that fine particles contribute most to moisture sorption due to their greater specific surface area; removing fines by sieving substantially reduced vapor uptake (pqac-00000027). Ti-6Al-4V, with its spherical and homogeneous particle morphology, shows very low moisture pickup in all tested states, indicating much lower sorption susceptibility (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). Nevertheless, even Ti-6Al-4V can form moisture-mediated agglomerates via capillary bridges (pqac-00000023). Drying practices in the literature typically use 80–190 °C, with vacuum drying at 85 °C for 12 hours producing effective moisture removal (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000024).

Pharmaceutical powders such as lactose are particularly susceptible to humidity-induced caking. The caking mechanism involves condensation, dissolution, and recrystallization at particle contacts, driven by the difference between ambient RH and the material's critical RH or DRH (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046). ### Summary and Practical Recommendations

For **test (6)**, the saturated-salt humidity chambers provide thermodynamic fixed points with Greenspan-tabulated uncertainties of ±0.1–0.5% RH at 25 °C (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000069). Temperature control to ±0.5 °C is advisable, particularly for Mg(NO₃)₂ whose dRH/dT is approximately −0.3% RH/°C (pqac-00000069). Including a small circulating fan reduces equilibration time by 10–50× (pqac-00000062). After opening a chamber to load or remove a sample, re-equilibration with fan assistance should be verified by monitoring the SHT45 sensor until readings stabilize to within ±0.5% RH. For gravimetric sorption on a few grams of powder, thin layers (< ~1 mm) on the balance pan will help ensure that vapor diffusion is not rate-limiting, as agreement with DVS is good when bed diffusivity exceeds ~10⁻⁹ m²/s (pqac-00000047). NaCl powder should not be conditioned at the NaCl-saturated chamber (~75% RH) because this coincides with its own DRH, risking irreversible caking (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042). AlSi10Mg is the most moisture-sensitive of the metal AM powders and should be prioritized for humidity-dosing characterization (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028).

For **test (10)**, the Faraday cup should use a deep aluminium inner cup inside a grounded can, connected to a femtoampere-grade charge amplifier via guarded cabling (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000032). The LMP7721 (3 fA bias) or ADA4530-1 (~20 fA bias) are suitable op-amps for a home-built integrating charge amplifier, with feedback capacitor values chosen to match the expected charge range of ~0.1–100 nC per dose (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Driven guard traces, Teflon insulation, triaxial cables, and meticulous cleanliness are essential for meaningful sub-picoampere measurements (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000072). Expected charge-to-mass ratios from auger feeding through a PLA tube are likely in the 1–10 nC/g range for most powders, with significant humidity dependence (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000055). Pairing Faraday-cup measurements before and after humidity conditioning will provide a direct link between tests (6) and (10)."}

state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. For tests (6) and (10): what does the literature report on (a) saturated-salt humidity chambers (Greenspan 1977; ISO 12571; OIML): accuracy, temperature sensitivity, equilibration time after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, sample size and layer thickness for gravimetric sorption, agreement with dynamic vapour sorption, and humidity effects on the flow of NaCl (deliquescence near 75 % RH), metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V) and pharmaceutical powders, including caking; (b) Faraday-cup measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio of powders after feeding, conveying or sieving: cup and shield design, electrometers versus home-built charge amplifiers (op-amp choice, feedback capacitor, leakage, guarding), collection efficiency for fines, typical charge-to-mass ratios for salts, metal powders and organic powders after contact with polymers (PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon) and steel, and their humidity dependence.

## Literature Review for Tests (6) and (10): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Faraday-Cup Charge-to-Mass Ratio Measurement

---

### Part (a): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Humidity Effects on Powder Flow

#### 1. Accuracy of Saturated-Salt Humidity Fixed Points

The definitive reference for saturated-salt humidity fixed points is Greenspan (1977), who compiled equilibrium relative humidity (RH) data for 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions using 1,106 measurements from 21 investigations, fitted as polynomial functions of temperature (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 1-2, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 2-3). Uncertainties were assigned as three times the standard deviation of the predicted values, with individual datum uncertainties propagated through a root-sum-square combination of contributions from temperature, pressure, equilibrium attainment, and sensor calibration (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 7-8, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 6-7). At 25 °C, the reported uncertainties for salts commonly used in humidity chambers are: LiCl 11.3 ± 0.3% RH; MgCl₂ 32.8 ± 0.2% RH; Mg(NO₃)₂ 52.9 ± 0.2% RH; NaCl 75.3 ± 0.2% RH; KCl 84.3 ± 0.3% RH; KNO₃ 93.6 ± 0.6% RH; and K₂SO₄ 97.3 ± 0.5% RH (lu2007uncertaintyevaluationof pages 1-2, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5). Lu and Chen (2007) used these Greenspan values to calibrate humidity sensors with vessels maintained at 25 ± 0.2 °C and 12-hour equilibration periods, reporting that the dominant contribution to combined uncertainty was the predicted calibration uncertainty of the sensor itself rather than the salt reference (lu2007uncertaintyevaluationof pages 1-2).

The following table summarizes the Greenspan fixed points for the specific salts proposed in the user's setup:

| Salt / humidity medium | RH at 25 °C (%) | Uncertainty (±% RH) | Approx. dRH/dT at 25 °C (% RH/°C) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| MgCl₂ | 32.78 | 0.16 | −0.06 | Saturated magnesium chloride fixed point; suitable for the low-RH chamber. (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5) |
| Mg(NO₃)₂ | 52.89 | 0.22 | −0.30 | Most temperature-sensitive listed salt point; a ±1 °C change shifts nominal RH by approximately ∓0.30 percentage points. (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5) |
| NaCl | 75.29 | 0.12 | −0.07 | Fixed point lies near NaCl’s deliquescence threshold; unsuitable for conditioning NaCl powder if it must remain safely below deliquescence. (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5) |
| KCl | 84.34 | 0.26 | −0.15 | High-RH fixed point; temperature control and condensation avoidance are especially important. (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4) |
| Silica gel | ≈0–5 | Not a Greenspan fixed-point uncertainty | Not applicable | Desiccant, not a saturated binary salt solution. RH depends on regeneration, loading, leakage, and sample moisture; verify it with the chamber sensor. |


*Table: Greenspan humidity fixed points and approximate temperature coefficients for the proposed salt chambers. Silica gel is included separately because it is a variable desiccant rather than a thermodynamic fixed point.*

#### 2. Temperature Sensitivity

The temperature coefficient dRH/dT varies considerably among salts. From the polynomial coefficients in Greenspan's Table 1 (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 2-3, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4), NaCl has a relatively small temperature sensitivity of approximately −0.07% RH/°C near 25 °C, whereas Mg(NO₃)₂ is approximately −0.30% RH/°C—meaning that a ±1 °C temperature excursion shifts the nominal RH by ∓0.3 percentage points for Mg(NO₃)₂ but only ∓0.07 for NaCl. MgCl₂ has an even flatter coefficient (approximately −0.06% RH/°C), making it one of the most temperature-insensitive fixed points (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5). Rockland (1960) emphasized the desirability of salts with low temperature coefficients and warned that even small temperature variations can cause significant changes in equilibrium RH (rockland1960saturatedsaltsolutions pages 1-1). Rörig-Dalgaard and Svensson (2016) cautioned that heat of solution during salt dissolution or crystallization can locally change temperature and thus calibration RH, noting that inadequate moisture control can produce calibration uncertainty as large as ±2.5% RH (rorigdalgaard2016highaccuracycalibration pages 3-4).

#### 3. Equilibration Time and Effect of Mixing Fans

Equilibration time depends strongly on the salt, chamber volume, sample loading, and air circulation. In dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) calibration, salt-specific test durations ranged from approximately 6 hours for MgCl₂ to 20 hours for LiCl and KNO₃, with NaCl and Mg(NO₃)₂ requiring approximately 10 hours (rorigdalgaard2016highaccuracycalibration pages 6-8). For static desiccator-type chambers, equilibration can require days to weeks, particularly at high RH (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 1-5, imre1964themeasurementof pages 1-4). Rockland (1960) explicitly evaluated the effect of mechanical convection (a mixing fan) on equilibration rates and reported that fans decreased the time to achieve equilibration by 10 to 50 times compared to still-air conditions (rockland1960saturatedsaltsolutions pages 1-1). This strongly supports including a small circulating fan within each humidity chamber to accelerate recovery after opening.

#### 4. Sample Size and Layer Thickness for Gravimetric Sorption

Traditional saturated-salt-solution (SSS) gravimetric sorption methods typically require large samples of 10–100 g, with equilibration periods of days to weeks (burnettUnknownyearmoisturesorptionproperties pages 1-2). Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) instruments use much smaller samples, typically 20–100 mg, with equilibration at each RH step achievable in hours rather than days (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 5-9, munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 3-5). For the proposed few-gram setup using the doser, intermediate between these extremes, the key consideration is ensuring that the powder layer is thin enough for vapor to penetrate the bed rapidly. Arlabosse et al. (2003) found that for materials with apparent diffusion coefficients above approximately 10⁻⁹ m²/s, good agreement between static and dynamic methods was obtained; a 500 µm powder slab of microcrystalline cellulose gave diffusion coefficients of 1.7–4.4 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s and produced consistent results (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13, arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 5-9).

#### 5. Agreement Between DVS and Saturated-Salt Methods

Good agreement between DVS and SSS methods has been reported for several powder materials, particularly at low to intermediate RH. For microcrystalline cellulose, pharmaceutical granules, and barley straw, DVS and SSS isotherms generally agreed well (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13, bui2017comparisonofthe pages 6-9, bui2017comparisonofthe pages 1-6). Disagreement can arise at high water activity (above ~0.6–0.8) where slow internal diffusion limits the sample's ability to reach thermodynamic equilibrium within DVS step times (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13). The DVS mass-stability criterion is typically 100 times less stringent than the SSS criterion, which partly accounts for DVS being faster but potentially less accurate at high RH (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 5-9). For materials with dense or laminated structures, the methods may disagree because DVS results become dependent on sorption rate rather than thermodynamic equilibrium (schmidt2012comparisonbetweenwater pages 1-4).

#### 6. Humidity Effects on NaCl (Deliquescence Near 75% RH)

Sodium chloride has a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75–76% at 25 °C (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33). Below this threshold, the crystalline phase is thermodynamically stable; at or above DRH, water uptake initiates dissolution and formation of a saturated aqueous solution. The dissolution rate is proportional to the difference between imposed RH and DRH (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 3-4). At 80% RH, approximately 25.5% of NaCl dissolves after four days; at 85% RH, 57.3%; and at 90% RH, 80.3% (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 6-9). Operating at exactly 75% RH places NaCl dangerously close to its DRH: small temperature or humidity fluctuations can trigger partial dissolution, formation of liquid bridges at particle contacts, and subsequent recrystallization upon drying, producing solid bridges and irreversible caking (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33). Dense NaCl powder aggregates can take days or weeks to deliquesce completely because vapor transport is restricted within the powder bed (linnow2006investigationofsodium pages 58-61, linnow2006investigationofsodium pages 54-58). This suggests that the NaCl chamber should ideally be omitted for conditioning NaCl powder itself, as the equilibrium RH of saturated NaCl coincides with NaCl's own DRH.

#### 7. Humidity Effects on Metal AM Powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V)

Among metal AM powders, AlSi10Mg is the most susceptible to moisture uptake, with moisture content increasing up to six times the initial value after conditioning at 50 °C and 80% RH for 72 hours (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 1-2). The irregular and rough particle morphology of AlSi10Mg promotes moisture adsorption through both physisorption and chemisorption, leading to thicker oxide layers, agglomeration via capillary bridges, and severely degraded spreadability (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 2-3). DVS measurements on similar AlSi7Mg powders showed that fine particles contribute most to moisture sorption due to their greater specific surface area; removing fines by sieving substantially reduced vapor uptake (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 5-8). Ti-6Al-4V, with its spherical and homogeneous particle morphology, shows very low moisture pickup in all tested states, indicating much lower sorption susceptibility (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 4-5). Nevertheless, even Ti-6Al-4V can form moisture-mediated agglomerates via capillary bridges (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11). Drying practices in the literature typically use 80–190 °C, with vacuum drying at 85 °C for 12 hours producing effective moisture removal (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 4-5, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 2-3).

#### 8. Humidity Effects on Pharmaceutical Powders and Caking

Pharmaceutical powders such as lactose are particularly susceptible to humidity-induced caking. Amorphous fractions within otherwise crystalline powders are hygroscopic and can crystallize when exposed to humid air, releasing water and forming solid bridges (afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 39-43). The caking mechanism involves condensation, dissolution, and recrystallization at particle contacts, driven by the difference between ambient RH and the material's critical RH or DRH (afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33, afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 39-43). Caking strength correlates with the rate and extent of crystallization, and repeated humidity cycling generally worsens the effect. Storage of hygroscopic powders over saturated solutions of MgCl₂, NaBr, NaCl, and KCl has been used to study caking at controlled RH levels (afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33).

---

### Part (b): Faraday-Cup Measurement of Powder Charge-to-Mass Ratio

#### 1. Cup and Shield Design

The standard Faraday cup for powder charge measurement consists of a conducting inner measurement cup surrounded by a larger grounded conducting outer cup, with an electrically insulating material (typically Teflon) separating them (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7, sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114, cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51). The outer cup functions as a Faraday cage, reducing electromagnetic background noise (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51, sowinski2012thestudyof pages 56-59). A BNC or coaxial cable connects the assembly to the measurement electronics: the cable shield connects to the grounded outer cup, while the center conductor connects to the inner cup (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51, cruise2023triboelectricchargingofb pages 47-51). Very high insulation between the inner and outer cups is required to minimize charge decay (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7). Sowinski (2012) described concentric cylindrical copper vessels with inner dimensions of 0.15 m diameter × 0.25 m height and outer dimensions of 0.20 m diameter × 0.33 m height, isolated by Teflon bolts and connected to a Keithley 6514 electrometer (sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114). For the proposed bench-top setup with a 3 mm doser outlet, a smaller aluminium cup inside a grounded can is appropriate.

#### 2. Collection Efficiency for Fines

Collection efficiency for fine particles is a recognized challenge. Sowinski (2012) used a reusable filter bag with only 26–30% capture efficiency for 1 µm particulates (sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114). Sun et al. (2019) designed a mini-Faraday cup with an internal metal disc filter specifically to achieve high collection efficiency for charged ultrafine particles in the 50–300 nm range, with measured current showing good linearity with particle concentration (sun2019designandevaluation pages 6-7). For the proposed setup collecting auger-dosed powder, ensuring that all fine particles land in the cup rather than being lost to air currents or electrostatic adhesion to walls is important; a deep cup geometry and controlled drop height help maximize collection.

#### 3. Electrometers Versus Home-Built Charge Amplifiers

Commercial electrometers (e.g., Keithley 6514) provide turnkey charge/current measurement with proven specifications but at high cost (sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114). For a home-built charge amplifier, the critical component is an electrometer-grade CMOS op-amp with ultra-low input bias current (mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 4-6, mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 1-2). Two leading candidates are:

- **LMP7721** (Texas Instruments): 3 fA typical input bias current, 17 MHz gain-bandwidth product, rail-to-rail output. Its ultra-low bias current makes it suitable for sub-picoampere transimpedance and charge-integrator circuits (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 17-20, currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 22-25).
- **ADA4530-1** (Analog Devices): ~20 fA typical input bias current, designed specifically for electrometer applications with on-chip guarding (sharmaUnknownyearabootstrappedesd pages 51-57).

The charge amplifier operates as an integrator: a known feedback capacitor C_F between the output and inverting input converts input charge to voltage according to q = C_F × V_F (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51). The feedback capacitor value determines both sensitivity and dynamic range; smaller capacitors give higher sensitivity but saturate sooner. A parallel high-value resistor or periodic reset switch prevents drift from integrating bias current (mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 1-2). Input capacitance (~11 pF for LMP7721) combined with PCB stray capacitance forms a pole with feedback components that can cause instability; a feedback capacitor may be needed for compensation, with the value determined experimentally (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 17-20).

#### 4. Leakage, Guarding, and Practical Implementation

At femtoampere current levels, leakage from PCB traces, connectors, and insulation dominates measurement error (sharmaUnknownyearabootstrappedesd pages 51-57). Guarding is essential: a driven guard trace surrounds the high-impedance input and feedback nodes, maintained at approximately the same potential as the protected node, so that voltage differences across insulation are eliminated and leakage current is diverted into the low-impedance guard rather than the input (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22, mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 4-6). The guard should form a complete conductive enclosure including guard planes connected through vias, with an external ground plane or shield protecting it from noise and leakage (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22). Triaxial cables extend guarding along cables to the Faraday cup (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22). Cleanliness is critical for sub-picoamp performance: flux residues, moisture, solvents, and contamination degrade leakage performance; PCB materials with low moisture absorption should be selected, and solder mask should be removed around guard structures (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22, sharmaUnknownyearabootstrappedesd pages 51-57). Teflon is the preferred insulating material for ultra-low-leakage applications (mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 4-6). Supply filtering with a low-noise linear regulator, ~100 Ω series resistance, and ≥100 µF bypass capacitor is recommended to prevent supply noise from coupling through ESD capacitance (~0.5 pF) at each input (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 22-25).

#### 5. Typical Charge-to-Mass Ratios

The following table summarizes representative charge-to-mass ratios from the literature:

| Powder Type | Contact Material | Charge-to-Mass Ratio (nC/g) | Humidity Condition | Source |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| ABS granules | Stainless steel | −8.67 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| ABS granules | Stainless steel | −3.22 | Humid (~82% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| ABS granules | PLA | +0.85 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| ABS granules | PLA | +0.37 | Humid (~82% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| PE granules | Stainless steel | −4.67 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| PE granules | Stainless steel | −3.87 | Humid (~82% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| PE granules | PLA | −5.29 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| PP granules | Stainless steel | −2.61 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| PP granules | PLA | −3.48 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5) |
| Lactose | Plastic | +3.87 ± 0.48 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7) |
| Lactose | Metal | +0.72 ± 0.09 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7) |
| Salbutamol sulfate | Plastic | +7.14 ± 1.07 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7) |
| Salbutamol sulfate | Metal | +14.16 ± 1.72 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7) |
| Generic 50 µm particle | Various | ~100 (typical-handling order of magnitude; size- and density-dependent limiting value) | Dry | Bailey (1993) (bailey1993chargingofsolids pages 1-3) |
| Polyethylene in silo handling | Steel | ~1–10 | Variable | Bailey (1993) (bailey1993chargingofsolids pages 6-9) |


*Table: Reported net charge-to-mass ratios span roughly 1–100 nC/g and depend strongly on powder, contact material, process, and humidity. The paired Dani measurements show that humid conditioning generally reduced charge magnitude, but these values are comparators rather than transferable constants for the PLA auger.*

Bailey (1993) reported that a typical 50 µm spherical particle has a charge-to-mass ratio of approximately 10⁻⁴ C/kg (100 µC/kg = 100 nC/g), which is considered fairly typical for energetic powder-handling procedures (bailey1993chargingofsolids pages 1-3). Gentle operations such as sieving and pouring produce lower values in the range of approximately 1–10 nC/g (1–10 µC/kg), while pneumatic conveying and micronizing can generate substantially higher charging (bailey1993chargingofsolids pages 6-9). Dani et al. (2024) measured polymer granules charged in a vibratory device against stainless steel and PLA, reporting values of 1–9 nC/g depending on the polymer and recipient material (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5). For pharmaceutical powders, Peart (2001) reported lactose at +3.87 nC/g after plastic contact and salbutamol sulfate at +14.16 nC/g after metal contact (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7).

#### 6. Triboelectric Series Considerations for the PLA Auger

In the conventional triboelectric series, nylon is positioned on the strongly positive side, while PTFE (Teflon) is at the most negative extreme; polyethylene, polypropylene, and PVC occupy intermediate negative positions (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 2-4, prawatya2018multivariateoptimisationand pages 21-24). PLA, though not always explicitly listed in older triboelectric series, has been shown experimentally to charge polymers either positively or sign-reverse relative to stainless steel: ABS charged negatively against stainless steel but positively against PLA, while PE and PP charged negatively against both (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5). This sign reversal demonstrates that the PLA auger tube will produce different charging polarities than a stainless-steel auger for the same powder, which is directly measurable with the proposed Faraday cup.

#### 7. Humidity Dependence of Triboelectric Charging

Humidity has a profound effect on triboelectric charging through multiple mechanisms: (i) adsorbed water layers increase surface conductivity, enabling charge dissipation; (ii) water bridges between contacting surfaces facilitate ion-mediated charge transfer; (iii) the dielectric strength of humid air is reduced, lowering the saturation charge on particles (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 100-104, sutka2023engineeringpolymerinterfaces pages 5-5). Experimentally, Dani et al. (2024) found that humid conditioning (96 hours at 82% RH) reduced the absolute charge-to-mass ratio to approximately 50–70% of normal values across all tested polymers (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5). Schella et al. (2017) demonstrated that polymer granulates became highly charged at low humidity (<30% RH) but acquired almost no charge above 80% RH, with the transition RH depending on the material (sutka2023engineeringpolymerinterfaces pages 5-5). For polymer contacts, charging was found to reach a maximum near 30% RH and decrease above 40% RH (sutka2023engineeringpolymerinterfaces pages 5-5). Temperature control to ±0.5 °C is advisable, particularly for Mg(NO₃)₂ whose dRH/dT is approximately −0.3% RH/°C (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5). Including a small circulating fan reduces equilibration time by 10–50× (rockland1960saturatedsaltsolutions pages 1-1). After opening a chamber to load or remove a sample, re-equilibration with fan assistance should be verified by monitoring the SHT45 sensor until readings stabilize to within ±0.5% RH. For gravimetric sorption on a few grams of powder, thin layers (< ~1 mm) on the balance pan will help ensure that vapor diffusion is not rate-limiting, as agreement with DVS is good when bed diffusivity exceeds ~10⁻⁹ m²/s (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13). The LMP7721 (3 fA bias) or ADA4530-1 (~20 fA bias) are suitable op-amps for a home-built integrating charge amplifier, with feedback capacitor values chosen to match the expected charge range of ~0.1–100 nC per dose (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 17-20, currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 22-25). ## Literature Review for Tests (6) and (10): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Faraday-Cup Charge-to-Mass Ratio Measurement

---

### Part (a): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Humidity Effects on Powder Flow

#### 1. Accuracy of Saturated-Salt Humidity Fixed Points

The definitive reference for saturated-salt humidity fixed points is Greenspan (1977), who compiled equilibrium relative humidity (RH) data for 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions using 1,106 measurements from 21 investigations, fitted as polynomial functions of temperature (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000066). Uncertainties were assigned as three times the standard deviation of the predicted values, with individual datum uncertainties propagated through a root-sum-square combination of contributions from temperature, pressure, equilibrium attainment, and sensor calibration (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004). At 25 °C, the reported uncertainties for salts commonly used in humidity chambers are: LiCl 11.3 ± 0.3% RH; MgCl₂ 32.8 ± 0.2% RH; Mg(NO₃)₂ 52.9 ± 0.2% RH; NaCl 75.3 ± 0.2% RH; KCl 84.3 ± 0.3% RH; KNO₃ 93.6 ± 0.6% RH; and K₂SO₄ 97.3 ± 0.5% RH (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000069). Lu and Chen (2007) used these Greenspan values to calibrate humidity sensors with vessels maintained at 25 ± 0.2 °C and 12-hour equilibration periods, reporting that the dominant contribution to combined uncertainty was the predicted calibration uncertainty of the sensor itself rather than the salt reference (pqac-00000000).

The following table summarizes the Greenspan fixed points for the specific salts proposed in the user's setup:

| Salt / humidity medium | RH at 25 °C (%) | Uncertainty (±% RH) | Approx. dRH/dT at 25 °C (% RH/°C) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| MgCl₂ | 32.78 | 0.16 | −0.06 | Saturated magnesium chloride fixed point; suitable for the low-RH chamber. (pqac-00000067, pqac-00000069) |
| Mg(NO₃)₂ | 52.89 | 0.22 | −0.30 | Most temperature-sensitive listed salt point; a ±1 °C change shifts nominal RH by approximately ∓0.30 percentage points. (pqac-00000067, pqac-00000069) |
| NaCl | 75.29 | 0.12 | −0.07 | Fixed point lies near NaCl’s deliquescence threshold; unsuitable for conditioning NaCl powder if it must remain safely below deliquescence. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000069) |
| KCl | 84.34 | 0.26 | −0.15 | High-RH fixed point; temperature control and condensation avoidance are especially important. (pqac-00000067) |
| Silica gel | ≈0–5 | Not a Greenspan fixed-point uncertainty | Not applicable | Desiccant, not a saturated binary salt solution. RH depends on regeneration, loading, leakage, and sample moisture; verify it with the chamber sensor. |


*Table: Greenspan humidity fixed points and approximate temperature coefficients for the proposed salt chambers. Silica gel is included separately because it is a variable desiccant rather than a thermodynamic fixed point.*

#### 2. Temperature Sensitivity

The temperature coefficient dRH/dT varies considerably among salts. From the polynomial coefficients in Greenspan's Table 1 (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067), NaCl has a relatively small temperature sensitivity of approximately −0.07% RH/°C near 25 °C, whereas Mg(NO₃)₂ is approximately −0.30% RH/°C—meaning that a ±1 °C temperature excursion shifts the nominal RH by ∓0.3 percentage points for Mg(NO₃)₂ but only ∓0.07 for NaCl. MgCl₂ has an even flatter coefficient (approximately −0.06% RH/°C), making it one of the most temperature-insensitive fixed points (pqac-00000069). Rockland (1960) emphasized the desirability of salts with low temperature coefficients and warned that even small temperature variations can cause significant changes in equilibrium RH (pqac-00000062). Rörig-Dalgaard and Svensson (2016) cautioned that heat of solution during salt dissolution or crystallization can locally change temperature and thus calibration RH, noting that inadequate moisture control can produce calibration uncertainty as large as ±2.5% RH (pqac-00000065).

#### 3. Equilibration Time and Effect of Mixing Fans

Equilibration time depends strongly on the salt, chamber volume, sample loading, and air circulation. In dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) calibration, salt-specific test durations ranged from approximately 6 hours for MgCl₂ to 20 hours for LiCl and KNO₃, with NaCl and Mg(NO₃)₂ requiring approximately 10 hours (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000064). For static desiccator-type chambers, equilibration can require days to weeks, particularly at high RH (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000063). Rockland (1960) explicitly evaluated the effect of mechanical convection (a mixing fan) on equilibration rates and reported that fans decreased the time to achieve equilibration by 10 to 50 times compared to still-air conditions (pqac-00000062). This strongly supports including a small circulating fan within each humidity chamber to accelerate recovery after opening.

#### 4. Sample Size and Layer Thickness for Gravimetric Sorption

Traditional saturated-salt-solution (SSS) gravimetric sorption methods typically require large samples of 10–100 g, with equilibration periods of days to weeks (pqac-00000054). Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) instruments use much smaller samples, typically 20–100 mg, with equilibration at each RH step achievable in hours rather than days (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000026). For the proposed few-gram setup using the doser, intermediate between these extremes, the key consideration is ensuring that the powder layer is thin enough for vapor to penetrate the bed rapidly. Arlabosse et al. (2003) found that for materials with apparent diffusion coefficients above approximately 10⁻⁹ m²/s, good agreement between static and dynamic methods was obtained; a 500 µm powder slab of microcrystalline cellulose gave diffusion coefficients of 1.7–4.4 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s and produced consistent results (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

#### 5. Agreement Between DVS and Saturated-Salt Methods

Good agreement between DVS and SSS methods has been reported for several powder materials, particularly at low to intermediate RH. For microcrystalline cellulose, pharmaceutical granules, and barley straw, DVS and SSS isotherms generally agreed well (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000051). Disagreement can arise at high water activity (above ~0.6–0.8) where slow internal diffusion limits the sample's ability to reach thermodynamic equilibrium within DVS step times (pqac-00000047). The DVS mass-stability criterion is typically 100 times less stringent than the SSS criterion, which partly accounts for DVS being faster but potentially less accurate at high RH (pqac-00000049). For materials with dense or laminated structures, the methods may disagree because DVS results become dependent on sorption rate rather than thermodynamic equilibrium (pqac-00000053).

#### 6. Humidity Effects on NaCl (Deliquescence Near 75% RH)

Sodium chloride has a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75–76% at 25 °C (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042). Below this threshold, the crystalline phase is thermodynamically stable; at or above DRH, water uptake initiates dissolution and formation of a saturated aqueous solution. The dissolution rate is proportional to the difference between imposed RH and DRH (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). At 80% RH, approximately 25.5% of NaCl dissolves after four days; at 85% RH, 57.3%; and at 90% RH, 80.3% (pqac-00000041). Operating at exactly 75% RH places NaCl dangerously close to its DRH: small temperature or humidity fluctuations can trigger partial dissolution, formation of liquid bridges at particle contacts, and subsequent recrystallization upon drying, producing solid bridges and irreversible caking (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000042). Dense NaCl powder aggregates can take days or weeks to deliquesce completely because vapor transport is restricted within the powder bed (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). This suggests that the NaCl chamber should ideally be omitted for conditioning NaCl powder itself, as the equilibrium RH of saturated NaCl coincides with NaCl's own DRH.

#### 7. Humidity Effects on Metal AM Powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V)

Among metal AM powders, AlSi10Mg is the most susceptible to moisture uptake, with moisture content increasing up to six times the initial value after conditioning at 50 °C and 80% RH for 72 hours (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028). The irregular and rough particle morphology of AlSi10Mg promotes moisture adsorption through both physisorption and chemisorption, leading to thicker oxide layers, agglomeration via capillary bridges, and severely degraded spreadability (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024). DVS measurements on similar AlSi7Mg powders showed that fine particles contribute most to moisture sorption due to their greater specific surface area; removing fines by sieving substantially reduced vapor uptake (pqac-00000027). Ti-6Al-4V, with its spherical and homogeneous particle morphology, shows very low moisture pickup in all tested states, indicating much lower sorption susceptibility (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). Nevertheless, even Ti-6Al-4V can form moisture-mediated agglomerates via capillary bridges (pqac-00000023). Drying practices in the literature typically use 80–190 °C, with vacuum drying at 85 °C for 12 hours producing effective moisture removal (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000024).

#### 8. Humidity Effects on Pharmaceutical Powders and Caking

Pharmaceutical powders such as lactose are particularly susceptible to humidity-induced caking. Amorphous fractions within otherwise crystalline powders are hygroscopic and can crystallize when exposed to humid air, releasing water and forming solid bridges (pqac-00000046). The caking mechanism involves condensation, dissolution, and recrystallization at particle contacts, driven by the difference between ambient RH and the material's critical RH or DRH (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000046). Caking strength correlates with the rate and extent of crystallization, and repeated humidity cycling generally worsens the effect. Storage of hygroscopic powders over saturated solutions of MgCl₂, NaBr, NaCl, and KCl has been used to study caking at controlled RH levels (pqac-00000042).

---

### Part (b): Faraday-Cup Measurement of Powder Charge-to-Mass Ratio

#### 1. Cup and Shield Design

The standard Faraday cup for powder charge measurement consists of a conducting inner measurement cup surrounded by a larger grounded conducting outer cup, with an electrically insulating material (typically Teflon) separating them (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The outer cup functions as a Faraday cage, reducing electromagnetic background noise (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013). A BNC or coaxial cable connects the assembly to the measurement electronics: the cable shield connects to the grounded outer cup, while the center conductor connects to the inner cup (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). Very high insulation between the inner and outer cups is required to minimize charge decay (pqac-00000008). Sowinski (2012) described concentric cylindrical copper vessels with inner dimensions of 0.15 m diameter × 0.25 m height and outer dimensions of 0.20 m diameter × 0.33 m height, isolated by Teflon bolts and connected to a Keithley 6514 electrometer (pqac-00000009). For the proposed bench-top setup with a 3 mm doser outlet, a smaller aluminium cup inside a grounded can is appropriate.

#### 2. Collection Efficiency for Fines

Collection efficiency for fine particles is a recognized challenge. Sowinski (2012) used a reusable filter bag with only 26–30% capture efficiency for 1 µm particulates (pqac-00000009). Sun et al. (2019) designed a mini-Faraday cup with an internal metal disc filter specifically to achieve high collection efficiency for charged ultrafine particles in the 50–300 nm range, with measured current showing good linearity with particle concentration (pqac-00000014). For the proposed setup collecting auger-dosed powder, ensuring that all fine particles land in the cup rather than being lost to air currents or electrostatic adhesion to walls is important; a deep cup geometry and controlled drop height help maximize collection.

#### 3. Electrometers Versus Home-Built Charge Amplifiers

Commercial electrometers (e.g., Keithley 6514) provide turnkey charge/current measurement with proven specifications but at high cost (pqac-00000009). For a home-built charge amplifier, the critical component is an electrometer-grade CMOS op-amp with ultra-low input bias current (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). Two leading candidates are:

- **LMP7721** (Texas Instruments): 3 fA typical input bias current, 17 MHz gain-bandwidth product, rail-to-rail output. Its ultra-low bias current makes it suitable for sub-picoampere transimpedance and charge-integrator circuits (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).
- **ADA4530-1** (Analog Devices): ~20 fA typical input bias current, designed specifically for electrometer applications with on-chip guarding (pqac-00000036).

The charge amplifier operates as an integrator: a known feedback capacitor C_F between the output and inverting input converts input charge to voltage according to q = C_F × V_F (pqac-00000070). The feedback capacitor value determines both sensitivity and dynamic range; smaller capacitors give higher sensitivity but saturate sooner. A parallel high-value resistor or periodic reset switch prevents drift from integrating bias current (pqac-00000037). Input capacitance (~11 pF for LMP7721) combined with PCB stray capacitance forms a pole with feedback components that can cause instability; a feedback capacitor may be needed for compensation, with the value determined experimentally (pqac-00000031).

#### 4. Leakage, Guarding, and Practical Implementation

At femtoampere current levels, leakage from PCB traces, connectors, and insulation dominates measurement error (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000074). Guarding is essential: a driven guard trace surrounds the high-impedance input and feedback nodes, maintained at approximately the same potential as the protected node, so that voltage differences across insulation are eliminated and leakage current is diverted into the low-impedance guard rather than the input (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000072). The guard should form a complete conductive enclosure including guard planes connected through vias, with an external ground plane or shield protecting it from noise and leakage (pqac-00000032). Triaxial cables extend guarding along cables to the Faraday cup (pqac-00000032). Cleanliness is critical for sub-picoamp performance: flux residues, moisture, solvents, and contamination degrade leakage performance; PCB materials with low moisture absorption should be selected, and solder mask should be removed around guard structures (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000074). Teflon is the preferred insulating material for ultra-low-leakage applications (pqac-00000072). Supply filtering with a low-noise linear regulator, ~100 Ω series resistance, and ≥100 µF bypass capacitor is recommended to prevent supply noise from coupling through ESD capacitance (~0.5 pF) at each input (pqac-00000033).

#### 5. Typical Charge-to-Mass Ratios

The following table summarizes representative charge-to-mass ratios from the literature:

| Powder Type | Contact Material | Charge-to-Mass Ratio (nC/g) | Humidity Condition | Source |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| ABS granules | Stainless steel | −8.67 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| ABS granules | Stainless steel | −3.22 | Humid (~82% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| ABS granules | PLA | +0.85 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| ABS granules | PLA | +0.37 | Humid (~82% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| PE granules | Stainless steel | −4.67 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| PE granules | Stainless steel | −3.87 | Humid (~82% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| PE granules | PLA | −5.29 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| PP granules | Stainless steel | −2.61 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| PP granules | PLA | −3.48 | Normal (~40% RH) | Dani et al. (2024) (pqac-00000016) |
| Lactose | Plastic | +3.87 ± 0.48 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (pqac-00000008) |
| Lactose | Metal | +0.72 ± 0.09 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (pqac-00000008) |
| Salbutamol sulfate | Plastic | +7.14 ± 1.07 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (pqac-00000008) |
| Salbutamol sulfate | Metal | +14.16 ± 1.72 | Ambient | Peart (2001) (pqac-00000008) |
| Generic 50 µm particle | Various | ~100 (typical-handling order of magnitude; size- and density-dependent limiting value) | Dry | Bailey (1993) (pqac-00000056) |
| Polyethylene in silo handling | Steel | ~1–10 | Variable | Bailey (1993) (pqac-00000055) |


*Table: Reported net charge-to-mass ratios span roughly 1–100 nC/g and depend strongly on powder, contact material, process, and humidity. The paired Dani measurements show that humid conditioning generally reduced charge magnitude, but these values are comparators rather than transferable constants for the PLA auger.*

Bailey (1993) reported that a typical 50 µm spherical particle has a charge-to-mass ratio of approximately 10⁻⁴ C/kg (100 µC/kg = 100 nC/g), which is considered fairly typical for energetic powder-handling procedures (pqac-00000056). Gentle operations such as sieving and pouring produce lower values in the range of approximately 1–10 nC/g (1–10 µC/kg), while pneumatic conveying and micronizing can generate substantially higher charging (pqac-00000055). Dani et al. (2024) measured polymer granules charged in a vibratory device against stainless steel and PLA, reporting values of 1–9 nC/g depending on the polymer and recipient material (pqac-00000016). For pharmaceutical powders, Peart (2001) reported lactose at +3.87 nC/g after plastic contact and salbutamol sulfate at +14.16 nC/g after metal contact (pqac-00000008).

#### 6. Triboelectric Series Considerations for the PLA Auger

In the conventional triboelectric series, nylon is positioned on the strongly positive side, while PTFE (Teflon) is at the most negative extreme; polyethylene, polypropylene, and PVC occupy intermediate negative positions (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059). PLA, though not always explicitly listed in older triboelectric series, has been shown experimentally to charge polymers either positively or sign-reverse relative to stainless steel: ABS charged negatively against stainless steel but positively against PLA, while PE and PP charged negatively against both (pqac-00000016). This sign reversal demonstrates that the PLA auger tube will produce different charging polarities than a stainless-steel auger for the same powder, which is directly measurable with the proposed Faraday cup.

#### 7. Humidity Dependence of Triboelectric Charging

Humidity has a profound effect on triboelectric charging through multiple mechanisms: (i) adsorbed water layers increase surface conductivity, enabling charge dissipation; (ii) water bridges between contacting surfaces facilitate ion-mediated charge transfer; (iii) the dielectric strength of humid air is reduced, lowering the saturation charge on particles (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020). Experimentally, Dani et al. (2024) found that humid conditioning (96 hours at 82% RH) reduced the absolute charge-to-mass ratio to approximately 50–70% of normal values across all tested polymers (pqac-00000016). Schella et al. (2017) demonstrated that polymer granulates became highly charged at low humidity (<30% RH) but acquired almost no charge above 80% RH, with the transition RH depending on the material (pqac-00000020). These findings indicate that the Faraday cup measurements should be performed at controlled and recorded humidity, ideally pairing them with the humidity chambers from test (6) to systematically map the charge–humidity relationship for each powder.

---

### Summary and Practical Recommendations

For **test (6)**, the saturated-salt humidity chambers provide thermodynamic fixed points with Greenspan-tabulated uncertainties of ±0.1–0.5% RH at 25 °C (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000069). Temperature control to ±0.5 °C is advisable, particularly for Mg(NO₃)₂ whose dRH/dT is approximately −0.3% RH/°C (pqac-00000069). Including a small circulating fan reduces equilibration time by 10–50× (pqac-00000062). For **test (10)**, the Faraday cup should use a deep aluminium inner cup inside a grounded can, connected to a femtoampere-grade charge amplifier via guarded cabling (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000032). The LMP7721 (3 fA bias) or ADA4530-1 (~20 fA bias) are suitable op-amps for a home-built integrating charge amplifier, with feedback capacitor values chosen to match the expected charge range of ~0.1–100 nC per dose (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide numerical values for the accuracy, temperature sensitivity (dRH/dT), or equilibrium time of saturated salt solutions. It does describe Greenspan’s uncertainty treatment for the compiled relative-humidity fixed-point data. Fundamental measurements from each investigator were used to calculate the actual relative humidity for each datum. Temperatures were converted to IPTS-68 equivalents, and vapor-pressure data from equations or tables were likewise converted to updated sources. For relative-humidity sensor calibration measurements, the uncertainty budget included calibration uncertainty and temperature uncertainty. For isopiestic measurements, it included temperature differences, concentration determination, equilibrium uncertainty, and uncertainty in the reference-solution data. A composite uncertainty was calculated as the square root of the sum of the individual parameter uncertainties squared, i.e., a root-sum-square combination. Greenspan notes that the estimates combined subjective judgments with objective estimates, but that these judgments generally had only a minor effect on the reported relative humidities and total uncertainties. The excerpt also states that solution and water purity effects were not evaluated. Thus, it supports a qualitative description of uncertainty methodology, not numerical performance specifications or equilibration times.

contexts.context: Greenspan (1977) treats the accuracy of saturated-salt humidity values through an explicit uncertainty budget rather than assigning one universal accuracy, because uncertainty depends on the measurement method and its parameters. Individual contributions were obtained from investigators’ estimates when reasonable; otherwise Greenspan estimated them from the quality of the work and the state of the art. Contributions were propagated as the square root of the sum of squared relative-humidity uncertainties, with special treatment when parameters were correlated. For relative vapor-pressure measurements, temperature and pressure differences, and the degree of equilibrium achieved, were important; for sensor calibration, calibration and temperature uncertainties mattered; and for isopiestic measurements, temperature-difference uncertainty was relevant. The excerpt does not report a numerical dRH/dT (temperature sensitivity) or a general equilibrium time for saturated salt solutions. It does indicate that equilibrium attainment contributes to uncertainty, so equilibration time must be method- and apparatus-dependent rather than a universal property. The enhancement-factor treatment is considered reliable near or below one atmosphere total pressure, where the difference between enhancement factors over saturated solution and pure water is negligible. The tabulated results are compared with prior compilations, generally agreeing within composite uncertainty, with several listed exceptions.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes preparation accuracy and equilibration requirements for saturated salt solutions used to calibrate a dynamic vapor sorption instrument, but it does not provide numerical temperature sensitivities (dRH/dT) or summarize Greenspan (1977) uncertainties. Salt–water mixtures were prepared at 20 ± 1 °C, using approximately 25 mg of dry salt. The salt-to-water ratio was optimized visually and then validated from absorption/desorption measurements. Equilibrium was assessed by exposing the lump to RH above its equilibrium RH for 1 hour; the mass increase during this period reflected equilibration throughout the lump and partial dissolution. Reliable calibration required a linear mass-change/RH relationship, agreement between absorption and desorption equilibrium RH, and continuous mass change. Preparation precision depended on heat of solution: MgCl2 and Mg(NO3)2 showed deviations of about 0.9% and 1.1% added water, whereas LiCl and KNO3 had inaccuracies of about 2.1% and 2.3%, respectively. The text also states that RH should be changed slowly enough to allow equilibrium, with dRH/dt adjusted as necessary, but it gives no general equilibration time beyond the one-hour conditioning criterion. No information about Greenspan 1977 or uncertainty values from that source appears in the supplied excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes Greenspan’s framework for assessing the accuracy of saturated-salt humidity fixed points, but it does not provide numerical equilibrium times or explicit dRH/dT values. The compilation covers 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions with relative humidities of approximately 3–98%, using 1,106 measurements from 21 investigations. Relative humidity was fitted as a function of temperature by least-squares regular polynomial equations, with the fitting procedure limited to polynomial order three and data between 0 and 104 °C. For uncertainty estimation, Greenspan calculated the standard deviation of the predicted relative humidity for each datum, then fitted those standard deviations versus temperature with a quadratic equation. At any selected temperature, three times the resulting predicted standard deviation was reported as the estimated uncertainty in RH, subject to exceptions discussed later in the paper. The excerpt notes that equilibration can be affected by humidity sources or sinks and by the initial equilibration process, but it gives no duration or criterion for reaching equilibrium. Likewise, determining temperature sensitivity would require differentiating the tabulated or fitted RH-versus-temperature equations, which are not included in these pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes two Faraday-cup configurations for powder charge measurements. The bottom cup uses concentric cylindrical copper vessels: an electrically isolated inner vessel is separated from the grounded outer shield by Teflon bolts and is connected directly to a Keithley Model 6514 digital electrometer. Its inner and outer dimensions are 0.1524 m diameter by 0.2540 m height and 0.2032 m diameter by 0.3302 m height, respectively. The outer cup provides electrical shielding and remains grounded. The top cup follows the same principle, with a 0.13 m diameter, 0.20 m high inner copper cup suspended inside a grounded 0.15 m diameter, 0.26 m high outer cup using Nylon bolts; the inner cup is connected to the electrometer. It collects entrained particles for simultaneous charge and mass measurement. A reusable filter bag retains entrained material, and a dust-lock filter is used to prevent particles from escaping when gas flow stops or the bag is removed. The cited filter has 26–30% capture efficiency for 1 μm particulates, which provides only limited fine-particle collection information. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a Faraday cup for measuring the charge of individual powder particles and provides design guidance relevant to charge-to-mass measurements. The preferred construction is a conducting inner measurement cup enclosed by a larger grounded conducting outer cup, with an electrically insulating layer between them. The outer cup functions as a Faraday cage and reduces electromagnetic background noise. A BNC cable connects the assembly to the measurement electronics: its shield is connected to the grounded outer cup, while its centre conductor connects to the inner cup. The inner cup is connected to a coulombmeter/electrometer, which detects the induced current when a charged particle enters the cup. An integrating amplifier converts this current into charge according to q = C_F V_F. In operation, the particle charge is obtained from the magnitude of the step change in the electrometer reading; the excerpt gives an example of a PTFE particle producing a 4.1 nC step. The passage does not specify collection efficiency for fine powders, a particular cup aperture or shield geometry beyond the nested-cup arrangement, or typical charge-to-mass-ratio values. It notes that Faraday cups are most suitable when particle charge exceeds instrument background noise, whereas trajectory tracking may be preferable for very small particles with high specific charge.
