contexts.context: The excerpt describes a mini-Faraday-cup electrometer intended for measuring charged ultrafine particles, rather than powders or directly reported charge-to-mass ratios. Its geometry includes a cylindrical stainless-steel metal case, a filter holder, a Teflon insulating support, and an internal metal filter. The filter is electrically isolated from the case, and a spring-probe electrode provides the electrical connection while reducing problems caused by mechanical vibration. The stainless-steel construction was selected to reduce external electrical noise affecting weak signals. The text reports high particle collection efficiency in the design context, but it does not provide a numerical efficiency value. Performance was tested using charged particles, including 220 nm particles and particles spanning 50–300 nm. Measured current varied linearly with particle number concentration; the fitted slope was 1.43×10^-19, close to the elementary charge, with adjusted R-square above 0.98 and Pearson correlation above 0.99. For smaller particles, measured current differed more from calculated current, attributed to diffusion losses in the tube. Comparison with a commercial electrometer also showed good agreement, with a slope of 1.03. The excerpt does not specify an inner cup surrounded by a grounded outer shield, a powder charge-to-mass measurement procedure, or typical powder charge-to-mass-ratio values.

It describes a double-walled arrangement: an inner measurement cup is surrounded by a grounded outer cup, which acts as an electrical shield against external electric fields. The inner cup is electrically connected to an electrometer; the electrometer determines charge by measuring the voltage developed across a known capacitor. The text identifies this direct Faraday-cup method as the most reliable way to measure the charge of fluidizing particles, particularly because in-bed electrostatic probes can become coated with particles, disturb bed hydrodynamics, induce additional charging, and measure induced charges rather than simply the particles’ surface charge. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a Faraday well (cup) consisting of a brass inner measuring well surrounded by a brass outer well or grounded shield. The inner well is electrically connected to an electrometer through a shielded coaxial cable, while the outer well provides shielding. When a charged powder sample is introduced, an equal and opposite charge flows from ground to balance the charge in the well; the resulting charge on the electrometer capacitor is measured. Very high insulation between the inner and outer wells is required to minimize charge decay. After charge measurement, the powder is weighed, and results are reported as specific charge, q/m. The excerpt does not provide a general collection-efficiency value for fine particles. It does note that in corona-charged powder clouds only about 0.5% of available ions attach to particles, with 99.5% remaining free; this concerns coating systems and possible spurious measurements rather than Faraday-cup particle collection efficiency. Reported example specific charges include lactose at +3.87 ± 0.48 nC g−1 after plastic contact and +0.72 ± 0.09 nC g−1 after metal contact, and salbutamol sulfate at +7.14 ± 1.07 nC g−1 after plastic contact and +14.16 ± 1.72 nC g−1 after metal contact. The standard well measures net charge only and cannot distinguish bipolar powders.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that humidity changes triboelectric charging by causing polymer granules to adsorb water on their surfaces. This thin surface water layer improves contact between particles and contacting surfaces and may permit diffusion of mobile electric charges, thereby altering the measured charge-to-mass ratio. In experiments, ABS, PS, PE, and PP granules were stored for 96 hours at approximately 82% relative humidity and 19 °C; their water contents increased by at least 10%, with increases of roughly 40% for ABS and 75% for PS and PP. Charge-to-mass measurements were then made after charging in a vibratory device using PLA, PE, or ABS recipients and a Faraday pail. For the reported polymer granules, humidity generally changed the magnitude of charging, and the effect depended on the recipient material. The excerpt provides example Q/m values only for ABS, PS, and PE charged against stainless steel (listed as “Inox”) and PLA. It does not provide typical charge-to-mass ratios for salts, metal powders, or organic powders after contact with PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon, and stainless steel; those values would require another source or additional pages of the study.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that humidity strongly affects both the polarity and magnitude of triboelectric charging in powders. For polyethylene, dry conditions can produce bipolar charging: coarse particles become positive while fines become negative. At higher relative humidity, all particles tended to charge negatively, regardless of particle size. The excerpt notes particularly negative polyethylene charging above approximately 40% RH, whereas charging may become positive under dry conditions. Around 35% RH, bipolar charging produced an approximately zero net charge, reducing discharge and fire hazards. Humidity also affects charge dissipation because powder resistivity controls how quickly charge leaks away from bulk powder; high-resistivity powders can retain charge and develop hazardous surface potentials. More generally, charging behavior depends on particle size, contacting surface type, and relative humidity. For handling operations, the excerpt reports charge-to-mass ratios of roughly a few microcoulombs per kilogram in the cited silo experiments, while sieving and pouring generated approximately 10^-11 to 10^-9 C/kg and energetic operations such as micronising and pneumatic transfer generated approximately 10^-7 to 10^-? C/kg (the scanned exponent is unclear). However, this excerpt does not provide charge-to-mass ratios specifically for salts, metal powders, or organic powders after contact with PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon, or stainless steel.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains several ways humidity can reduce triboelectric charging of powders. Increased humidity may lower the dielectric strength of air, reducing the saturation charge on particles; smaller particles may show a larger reduction because they otherwise saturate at higher charge-density levels. Humidity also causes water molecules to adsorb onto particle surfaces. These water layers contain mobile ions such as hydroxide and hydronium, increasing surface conductivity. The resulting mobile charge can redistribute over the particle surface and promote passive dissipation to the air or discharge when the particle contacts ground or a conductor. Consequently, humidity can lower both the charging rate and the final saturation charge obtained during contact charging. Adsorbed water can form electrical double layers, with an immobile Stern layer and mobile Gouy-Chapman layer; interactions between these layers may also contribute to charge transfer through water bridges. contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses humidity-related flow and spreadability degradation in AlSi10Mg and Ti6Al4V powders, although it does not provide detailed DVS methodology or specific storage-condition recommendations. Moisture is adsorbed through both physisorption and chemisorption. Physisorption is associated with capillary forces and liquid bridges between particles; for micrometer-scale particles, the capillary force is reported to be largely independent of relative humidity once moisture is entrapped, allowing agglomerations to persist. AlSi10Mg, whose particles are more irregular and rough, readily takes up moisture. Its moisture content can become six times the initial value after moisturizing, exhibits substantial measurement variability, and is difficult to remove by drying. Moisture-related agglomeration, combined with irregular morphology and a wider particle-size distribution, obstructs the applicator aperture and produces nonuniform powder layers, lines, particle-free regions, and potentially manufacturing defects such as porosity and dimensional inconsistencies. Ti6Al4V has spherical, homogeneous particles and shows very low moisture pickup in all tested states, indicating lower sorption susceptibility. Nevertheless, moisturizing still causes agglomeration, consistent with capillary-bridge behavior. Vacuum and air drying are mentioned as treatments, but the excerpt does not quantify their effectiveness for Ti6Al4V or give controlled humidity storage limits.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to understanding humidity-related degradation of metal additive-manufacturing powder flow and spreadability, although it does not provide detailed numerical results specifically for AlSi10Mg or Ti-6Al-4V, nor does it explicitly describe dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) terminology. It explains that L-PBF requires both high flowability and high apparent density, while moisture trapped or adsorbed on powder particles reduces flowability during spreading and can lower powder-bed apparent density. Humidity may also promote growth of aluminum’s native oxide film; the oxide reaches approximately 4–10 nm in total thickness over weeks or months, with thicker films possible in humid environments. The authors propose direct moisture-content measurement using a moisture analyzer, analogous to thermogravimetric analysis, because conventional oxygen and nitrogen measurements do not directly quantify surface moisture. Standard Carney and Hall flowmeters are considered unsuitable for very fine, irregular, or moisturized powders, while the proposed thin-layer tools more closely reproduce L-PBF recoating and quantify spreadability and apparent density. The study conditions powders as-received, air-dried, vacuum-dried, and moisturized, enabling comparison of storage or environmental moisture states. Moisture may additionally cause hydrogen porosity during melting, and prior studies suggest pre-drying can reduce pores and increase relative density. Drying practices in the literature vary, commonly using 80–190 °C, often in air, with contamination concerns.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general evidence relevant to studying humidity effects on metal additive-manufacturing powders, although it concerns Al 5056 and tantalum rather than AlSi10Mg or Ti-6Al-4V and does not report DVS measurements or spreadability directly. Moisture content is identified as an important factor affecting powder flowability. In experiments involving repeated exposure to humid laboratory conditions, moisture and flowability data were scattered, and no clear monotonic relationship with exposure number or duration was established. For Al 5056, the longer 10-minute exposures generally produced moisture values comparable to or higher than those from 2-minute exposures, consistent with greater exposure to humidity. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an experimental framework for evaluating how humidity conditioning affects metal-powder flowability, apparent density, moisture content, and spreadability in additive manufacturing. Four powder states were compared: as-received, vacuum-dried at 85 °C for 12 hours under less than 10−2 mbar, air-dried at 150 °C for 20 minutes, and moisturized at 50 °C and 80% relative humidity for 72 hours. Drying temperatures were selected to ensure complete moisture removal, while the humidity treatment produced a conditioned, moisture-exposed state. Because drying and moisturizing could create agglomerates, samples were mixed for 10 minutes before flowability testing. Spreadability was measured using applicator tools depositing a nominal 100 μm-thick and 20 mm-wide powder layer; deposited volume and powder mass were used to calculate apparent density. Flowability was also assessed with Hall-flow measurements, recording the time for 50 g of powder to pass through a 2.54 mm aperture, alongside relative density. Moisture uptake was quantified by mass loss during heating to 150 °C. SEM examination found no observable morphology differences among as-received, dried, and moisturized powders. contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant evidence on how particle size distribution and humidity-related moisture sorption can affect metal additive-manufacturing powder flow and spreading, although it concerns AlSi7Mg rather than the specifically requested AlSi10Mg and Ti-6Al-4V powders. Powders A and B had relatively spherical particles, narrow particle-size distributions, and better flowability, whereas powder C contained finer particles, irregular larger particles, satellites, and a broad distribution (D10 = 14 µm, D50 = 31 µm, D90 = 58 µm). Powder C did not flow through the Hall funnel and required 15.3 ± 0.4 s/50 g through the Carney funnel, compared with approximately 6.1 s/50 g for powders A and B. Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) showed substantially greater moisture uptake for powder C. Removing its fine fraction by sieving reduced vapor sorption, indicating that fine particles and their greater surface area contribute strongly to humidity sensitivity. The authors also performed repeated flowability measurements at 40% relative humidity using 50 g of dried powder, specifically to evaluate humidity effects on flow. For spreading, powder C produced lower spread density and showed particle segregation across the powder bed, while trapped gas was observed in powders A and B. contexts.context: At 25°C, sodium chloride has a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75%. Below this threshold, the crystalline phase is thermodynamically favored; at or above it, water uptake and formation of an aqueous salt solution become favorable. For powder flow and storage, increasing humidity can promote capillary condensation at particle contact points, creating liquid bridges. These bridges dissolve NaCl locally and can initiate particle agglomeration and caking. If environmental humidity or temperature subsequently changes and water evaporates, the saturated or supersaturated solution recrystallizes, producing solid bridges that generally bind particles more strongly than liquid bridges. The resulting cake strength depends on temperature, humidity, pressure, mass transfer, powder solubility, and the number of particle contact points. Kinetically, the study reports that NaCl dissolution under controlled conditions increases with the humidity driving force: the dissolution rate is proportional to the difference between imposed RH and the DRH. Dynamic Vapor Sorption measurements can track water uptake during deliquescence and water loss during recrystallization. In contrast, evaporation and recrystallization are not described by the same simple relationship; they appear to depend on more complex crystal-growth processes from a supersaturated salt solution. Small particles may dissolve before larger agglomerates, producing nonequilibrium behavior within a powder bed.
contexts.question: NaCl deliquescence at 75% RH: effect on powder flow, caking mechanism, dissolution and recrystallization kinetics

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies sodium chloride’s deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) as approximately 75–76% RH under the stated conditions. Above this threshold, water vapor uptake and capillary condensation produce liquid at crystal contacts, enabling NaCl dissolution; below the DRH, lowering water-vapor pressure promotes recrystallization. This provides the basis for understanding humidity-driven changes in powder flow: condensed liquid bridges connect particles and initiate caking, which can impair powder mobility and handling. Environmental scanning electron microscopy is used to observe wetting and drying, while dynamic vapor sorption measures mass uptake and its rate. The proposed kinetic model applies Knudsen gas-kinetic theory, relating the net water-molecule flux to the difference between imposed vapor pressure or water activity and the saturated-solution value. Experiments used millimeter-scale NaCl crystals at controlled temperature and humidity; at 2°C, changing water-vapor pressure between approximately 3 and 5 Torr produced conditions above or below the roughly 75% DRH. At 72% RH, liquid at crystal contacts was too small to observe microscopically, whereas at 83% RH a substantial condensed liquid volume and wetting of the crystal surfaces were visible. The resulting saturated solution and liquid bridges constitute the initial structural mechanism of caking.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes how NaCl powder responds as relative humidity approaches or exceeds its deliquescence relative humidity (DRH), which is relevant to behavior near 75% RH. Water uptake and loss are governed by the difference between imposed RH and DRH: closer to or above DRH, the rate of moisture uptake and dissolution increases, while below DRH evaporation and recrystallization occur. ESEM observations indicate that dissolution at high RH is relatively homogeneous, with individual crystals and aggregates taking up water simultaneously. The reported 25 °C data show strong RH dependence: after four days, 25.5% of NaCl dissolved at 80% RH, 57.3% at 85% RH, and 80.3% at 90% RH. Thus, a condition at 75% RH would be expected to produce substantially less dissolution than these measured conditions if it is below or only near the DRH, although the excerpt does not provide a direct 75% RH measurement. During drying below DRH, recrystallization proceeds through distinct stages: growth from partially dissolved aggregates and nucleation/growth from homogeneous solution formed by complete dissolution. These processes produce larger, more compact clusters and alter particle size and shape, providing the caking mechanism. The excerpt does not directly quantify powder-flow changes, but the observed aggregation and caking imply deterioration of flowability.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies NaCl’s deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) as approximately 76% RH at 25°C. Therefore, exposure to 75% RH is just below the deliquescence threshold: under stable conditions, substantial water uptake and severe caking are not expected, and storage below DRH is described as generally unproblematic. However, because 75% RH is very close to the threshold, small increases or humidity fluctuations could initiate capillary condensation and dissolution at particle contacts, potentially progressing toward deliquescence. This liquid phase promotes particle adhesion and can impair powder flow by creating liquid bridges and wet agglomerates. During subsequent drying, water evaporates and dissolved NaCl recrystallizes, producing solid bridges between particles and a persistent cake; repeated humidification-drying cycles can therefore worsen flowability and caking. The excerpt provides the qualitative sequence of condensation, dissolution, evaporation, and recrystallization, but it does not provide numerical dissolution or recrystallization rates, induction times, diffusion coefficients, or direct flowability measurements at exactly 75% RH. It also does not quantify how rapidly NaCl dissolves once the DRH is crossed or how quickly recrystallized bridges develop.

Bulk NaCl and NaCl-impregnated glass frits were compared to assess how confinement affects deliquescence rates. contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to NaCl deliquescence near 75% RH because it shows that deliquescence kinetics depend strongly on physical structure, not only on relative humidity. At or just above the equilibrium deliquescence humidity, the reaction slows substantially; experimentally, total reaction times increased as RH decreased toward the deliquescence threshold. Powder or crystal agglomerates deliquesce more slowly than isolated crystals because the initial liquid solution can occupy internal free space and have limited access to water vapor. This provides a plausible mechanism for powder caking: partial dissolution creates liquid bridges between particles, while compact packing, higher salt loading, smaller pores, and reduced vapor transport prolong the wet state and promote consolidation. The excerpt specifically reports that coarse bulk NaCl powder reacted more slowly than small crystals and that dense salt crusts could take days or weeks to deliquesce completely. In glass frits, the finest-pore specimen showed the slowest deliquescence, likely because its higher NaCl loading filled a larger fraction of available pores. The text does not directly quantify powder flowability, dissolution rates, or recrystallization kinetics. However, it supports the inference that restricted moisture transport and morphology-controlled dissolution govern the persistence of liquid phases; subsequent drying or RH reduction would be expected to enable recrystallization, although that process is not described here. Reported NaCl equilibrium deliquescence values correspond to approximately 75–78% RH at 25°C.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not discuss NaCl specifically or provide a quantitative deliquescence threshold at 75% RH, nor does it report dissolution or recrystallization rate constants. It does, however, provide a general framework applicable to a salt exposed above its deliquescence relative humidity. Moisture uptake can produce liquid or partially dissolved material at particle contacts; this increases particle mobility and flow, lowers resistance to deformation, and promotes liquid-bridge formation and agglomeration. The thermodynamic driving force is reduction of surface energy, while viscous resistance and external/mechanical forces influence the rate. If moisture subsequently decreases, the dissolved salt can dry and solidify, creating solid bridges and persistent caking. The passage emphasizes that caking is dynamic and proceeds slowly away from equilibrium, so equilibrium RH or water-content data alone cannot predict the time to cake. For NaCl at 75% RH, the relevant interpretation is therefore conditional: if 75% RH is above the powder’s effective deliquescence RH, deliquescence would cause surface dissolution, poorer flow, liquid-mediated agglomeration, and potentially recrystallized bridges during drying. Exact kinetics depend on temperature, particle size, contact geometry, liquid viscosity, mechanical stress, and RH history; these values are not supplied in the excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides kinetics and mechanistic information relevant to NaCl deliquescence near 75% RH, although the experiments were conducted at 78% RH and do not directly measure powder flow or caking. Deliquescence was monitored through the decline of NaCl X-ray diffraction peak intensities as crystalline salt dissolved. In bulk powder, dissolution remained incomplete after 25 hours, whereas porous glass substrates showed shorter apparent reaction times. However, the faster porous-substrate response reflects only the near-surface region observable by XRD; Cu Kα penetration was estimated at roughly 100–200 µm, and solution could migrate inward by capillary action, affecting the intensity curves. The authors attribute deliquescence rate to both dissolution of the crystal core into the initially formed solution film and water-vapor transfer from the atmosphere. Confinement in pores or powder aggregates reduces the gas–liquid interfacial area and restricts vapor access, so aggregates or confined crystals should deliquesce more slowly than isolated crystals. These observations support a caking mechanism in which humidity-induced surface liquid bridges or solution films promote particle adhesion, followed by continued dissolution. When RH decreases, recrystallization can occur and generate mechanical stress; the excerpt does not provide quantitative recrystallization-rate data or direct measurements of powder-flow changes.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents DVS as a faster alternative to the saturated salt solution (SSS) method because stabilization time depends directly on sample mass; lighter samples require shorter tests. However, reducing sample size can compromise representativeness, particularly for heterogeneous construction materials such as concrete. The SSS method is described as time-consuming but standardized under NF EN ISO 12570 and NF EN ISO 12571, whereas DVS lacks an applicable standard and commonly relies on manufacturer procedures, which may not suit every material. Previous comparisons generally found no significant difference or good agreement between DVS and SSS, although agreement is not universal. Discrepancies have been associated with slow vapor diffusion, differences in dry-state determination, and insufficient mass stabilization, especially at high relative humidity where adsorption kinetics are slower and moisture content may be underestimated. The excerpt does not provide specific numerical values for sample dimensions, layer thickness, or equilibration times, nor does it establish a direct effect of layer thickness. It emphasizes that sample representativeness, material heterogeneity, vapor permeability, dry-mass determination, and clearly defined protocols are critical when comparing the two techniques.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares DVS with the saturated-salts (static) method primarily through equilibrium assumptions, agreement, and time. Both methods are intended to establish thermodynamic equilibrium between the sample and surrounding atmosphere, but the DVS mass-stability criterion is substantially less stringent—reported as 100 times higher than the saturated-salts criterion. Consequently, DVS can produce an isotherm in a few days, whereas saturated salts may require several weeks. For microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) at 25°C, the methods agreed well: DVS results were consistent with the COST90 reference data, particularly at low water activity, and repeated DVS experiments showed good reproducibility. At water activity 0.9, saturated salts required approximately 7 days to equilibrate, while the complete DVS isotherm was obtained within 30 hours; DVS reached approximately 0.98 water activity after 6 hours but could not reach 1. A typical DVS sample was 20 mg. The excerpt does not give a general saturated-salt sample mass or a direct sample-layer thickness comparison. It does report a 500 µm MCC powder slab used for diffusion estimation, with diffusion coefficients of 1.7 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s at relative humidity 0.8 and 4.4 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s at another condition. The agreement is attributed to MCC’s poor adsorption, surface-dominated uptake, and relatively large bed diffusion coefficient.

contexts.context: This excerpt primarily describes the experimental procedures and apparatus for comparing saturated salt solution (SSS) and dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) measurements. For SSS, the procedure recommends at least three samples, a constant temperature, and at least five staged relative-humidity conditions. contexts.context: The excerpt supports a general comparison between dynamic vapor-sorption instruments, including DVS, and the conventional saturated-salt-slurry method, but it does not report specific DVS values for sample size, layer thickness, or equilibration time. Dynamic instruments continuously monitor sample weight while controlling relative humidity through mixtures of dry and water-vapor-saturated gas. They change humidity stepwise and hold the sample at each level until its weight falls within a predefined stability tolerance, thereby reducing manual handling and exposure to room conditions. The article’s Dynamic Dewpoint method, a related automated approach, produced sorption behavior similar to saturated-salt isotherms for four of five tested materials; corn flakes differed because slow diffusion through their dense laminated structure made results dependent on sorption rate and time. In contrast, saturated salt solutions provide accurate, temperature-dependent water activities and function as effectively infinite sinks, but generally require larger samples (typically over 1 g), repeated removal and weighing, and lengthy equilibration. The method also offers only the discrete water-activity values associated with available salts and may have mold-growth issues at high activity. Thus, the excerpt indicates broadly comparable isotherms, faster and less labor-intensive dynamic measurement, and potentially lower sample requirements, while emphasizing that kinetics, sample structure, and equilibration criteria can affect agreement. Layer thickness is not discussed.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares the dynamic DVS method with the static saturated-salt/COST 90 method across MCC powder, pharmaceutical granules, and a PEBA membrane. Agreement is good for MCC and pharmaceutical granules across the measured water-activity range, apparently because internal diffusion is not sufficiently limiting. For MCC, diffusion was evaluated using a 500 µm-thick powder slab; the estimated apparent diffusion coefficients were about 1.7 × 10^-9 m²/s at relative humidity 0.8 and 4.4 × 10^-9 m²/s at 0.2. The authors suggest that coefficients above approximately 10^-9 m²/s do not cause significant disagreement between static and dynamic measurements. For pharmaceutical granules, modeled as spheres with radius 0.625 mm, agreement was also good. Their relatively large diameter compared with the crucible prevented preparation of a powder layer, so transfer limitations could occur only within individual particles. Equilibration was much faster with DVS: approximately 5 hours versus 7 days for saturated salts at the highest water activity. For PEBA, agreement was good below water activity 0.6 but deteriorated at higher activity, where internal diffusion increasingly controlled sorption. DVS required about 19 hours, whereas saturated salts required about 12 days at 90% relative humidity and still may not have reached thermodynamic equilibrium.

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts conventional saturated-salt-solution measurements with Dynamic Vapour Sorption (DVS) primarily in terms of procedure, sample requirements, and equilibration. Traditional methods expose samples to saturated salt solutions at established relative humidities and periodically weigh them until equilibrium. The excerpt states that this static approach commonly requires many days or weeks, uses relatively large samples (typically 10–100 g), and can introduce weighing inaccuracies because samples must be removed from the storage container, potentially causing moisture gain or loss. DVS is presented as a rapid, sensitive, automated alternative that measures vapour uptake and loss gravimetrically, with a stated mass resolution of ±0.1 μg. Its vapour pressure is generated by mixing saturated and dry carrier-gas streams, while water-vapour concentration is actively measured and controlled in real time. The supplied text does not provide a direct quantitative comparison of agreement between DVS and saturated-salt isotherms, nor does it report specific layer-thickness requirements or numerical equilibration times for DVS. Thus, it supports comparison of general advantages and limitations, but not definitive conclusions about method-to-method isotherm agreement or the effects of sample layer thickness.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant primarily to pneumatic conveying and to the distinction between charge acquired during transport and charge retained after collection, but it does not provide the requested typical charge-to-mass ratios in nC/g or µC/kg. The study disperses powders into a gas stream, where particle-wall collisions in either a nylon cyclone or conductive steel-tube tribocharger generate charge. The reported inlet gas velocities through the tribochargers range from 10 to 20 m/s. Charge acquired during dispersion, Qd, is measured by integrating the current transferred to the steel tribocharger when the conductive tube is used. After transport, the powder settles into an insulated collecting cell inside a Faraday pail; integrating the Faraday-pail current gives Qs(t), the charge remaining in the settled powder. The authors explicitly distinguish Qd from Qs because charge can change during collection and settling. The excerpt contains no measurements or comparisons for sieving, pouring, or auger feeding, and it does not discuss the triboelectric-series positions of PLA, PTFE, nylon, or PETG. Although nylon is identified as a tribocharger material, that alone does not establish a polymer ranking or charge polarity for the requested materials.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides measured triboelectric charge-to-mass ratios for polymer granules in a vibratory device, expressed in nC/g; numerically, these values are equivalent to µC/kg. For ABS, values were −8.67 nC/g with an Inox recipient and +0.85 nC/g with PLA under normal conditions; after humid exposure they were −3.22 and +0.37 nC/g, respectively. PS measured −2.60 nC/g with Inox and −4.31 nC/g with PLA normally, changing to −1.44 and −3.46 nC/g when humid. PE measured −4.67 and −5.29 nC/g normally, and −3.87 and −4.37 nC/g when humid. PP measured −2.61 and −3.48 nC/g normally, and −1.87 and −2.39 nC/g when humid. Thus, the reported magnitudes are on the order of 1–10 nC/g (1–10 µC/kg), but the excerpt concerns vibratory charging rather than sieving, pouring, pneumatic conveying, or auger feeding. It does not provide triboelectric-series positions or charging data for PTFE, nylon, or PETG, and does not establish a general polymer ranking. Humidity reduced the absolute charge-to-mass ratio substantially, with humid granules retaining roughly 50%–70% of normal-condition values.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides charge-to-mass information for several powder-handling operations, although the scanned exponent notation is corrupted in places. It distinguishes relatively gentle operations, such as sieving and pouring, from energetic operations, such as micronising and pneumatic conveying, with the latter producing substantially greater triboelectric charging. In the cited full-scale silo experiments, measured silo current divided by powder mass-flow rate corresponded to charge-to-mass ratios of a few µC/kg, equivalent numerically to a few nC/g. The excerpt does not provide a specific value for auger feeding. It also emphasizes that powder charge depends strongly on electrical resistivity, particle size, contacting materials, mechanical energy, and relative humidity. For polyethylene, dry conditions could produce bipolar charging, with coarse particles positive and fines negative, whereas high humidity caused all particles to charge negatively; around 35% relative humidity, the net charge was approximately zero. The excerpt contains no triboelectric-series ranking or positional information for PLA, PTFE, nylon, or PETG, so those polymer positions cannot be supported from this passage.

It emphasizes that triboelectric charging depends on particle and surface properties—including size, shape, roughness, purity, permittivity, contact frequency, duration, and area—as well as temperature and relative humidity, so charge levels are strongly process- and condition-dependent. Repeated contact can reduce charge transfer toward a saturation level. The excerpt also describes size-dependent bipolar charging: a theoretical model predicts electron transfer from larger to smaller particles, with larger particles becoming positive and smaller particles negative; coarse polyethylene and fines reportedly showed this behavior in silo handling, while high humidity caused all particles to charge negatively. The included triboelectric series places nylon on the positive side of the listed materials, while polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, and Teflon are on the negative side; Teflon is shown as especially readily negative. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that equilibration of a saturated salt-water lump requires controlled humidity changes and sufficient time. In the calibration procedure, the chamber was maintained at RH above the salt solution’s equilibrium RH for one hour to ensure that the entire lump reached equilibrium; the associated mass increase reflected water uptake and partial salt dissolution. The chamber RH then needed to be changed slowly enough for the salt and surrounding air to equilibrate, with the rate of RH change adjusted as necessary. Equilibrium was assessed by comparing absorption and desorption behavior: under satisfactory conditions, the fitted lines coincided at the equilibrium point, corresponding to zero mass change. If the salt-water mixture was too wet or too dry, the intersection shifted away from the zero-mass-change point, providing a diagnostic of inadequate preparation. The excerpt does not provide a specific equilibration time after opening a humidity chamber, quantify the effect of a mixing fan, describe re-equilibration after an external disturbance, or discuss air circulation in a desiccator. It does note that dry salt was stored in a dry-climate desiccator below 5% RH before preparation, and that approximately 25 mg of salt was used to promote rapid equilibration while retaining measurement accuracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly report equilibration times for saturated salt humidity chambers after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, re-equilibration after disturbance, or air circulation in a desiccator. It instead describes airflow and humidity control in a dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) instrument. The test chamber receives a continuous, constant air flow adjustable from 100 to 200 SCCM/min, produced by mixing fully water-vapor-saturated air with very dry air. Vapor pressure is controlled either by open-loop mass-flow controllers or by closed-loop feedback from a dew point analyzer (DPA). Open-loop operation depends on calibration values and allows continuously controlled changes, whereas closed-loop operation uses the measured RH immediately before the sample chamber and adjusts the dry/moist air mixture. Closed-loop measurements show greater fluctuation around the target RH, although the RH corresponds to the DPA reading. The excerpt also emphasizes that heat from dissolution, crystallization, condensation, or evaporation can alter the local temperature and thereby affect equilibrium moisture measurements. These details may be relevant by analogy to air circulation and disturbance recovery, but no fan-specific or post-opening equilibration data are provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance on equilibration in humidity chambers but does not give a specific equilibration time after opening, quantify the effect of a mixing fan, or describe re-equilibration after a disturbance. It states that measurements are normally performed in a generally closed, thermostatically controlled chamber, using a sulfuric-acid or salt solution to establish the desired vapor tension. Equilibrium is identified operationally when consecutive sample-weight measurements remain constant, after which the chamber’s equilibrium relative humidity is determined. The system reaching equilibrium is not simply the salt solution and air: it includes the sample, air, and absorbent as a multicomponent system. During desorption, moisture transfers from the sample to the absorbent through the ambient air, so the absorbent concentration changes as it takes up water. The excerpt also notes that, for a fixed-size sample, the time required to reach practically constant weight generally increases as the chamber’s vapor tension increases. These principles imply that opening the chamber or otherwise disturbing it would require waiting until the intended temperature and vapor-tension conditions are restored and verified, but the excerpt supplies no numerical waiting period or direct evidence about forced air circulation, fan operation, or desiccator air mixing.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly study saturated-salt humidity chambers after opening, mixing-fan effects, or re-equilibration in a desiccator. It does provide related information from dynamic vapor sorption calibration tests. Longer test durations reduce the influence of heat generated by dissolution on the chamber microclimate because the instrument maintains constant air flow; this improves the representativeness of the measured equilibrium relative humidity. The authors used a controlled sequence beginning with evaporation until RH fell below the salt solution’s equilibrium RH, followed by absorption, rather than relying on a single equilibration direction. Their optimized durations varied substantially by salt: LiCl and KNO3 required about 20 h, MgCl2 about 6 h, and Mg(NO3)2 and NaCl about 10 h, with an initial hour at the highest RH. The table reports RH rates and narrow operating intervals around the equilibrium RH, indicating that equilibration requirements depend strongly on salt properties. The text also states that approximately 3% water relative to solid salt mass was needed for each additional hour of sequence duration. These findings suggest that air circulation and extended waiting can help restore stable RH after a disturbance, but the excerpt gives no direct time constant or protocol for opening a chamber or using a mixing fan.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited information relevant to equilibration in humidity-controlled chambers, but it does not directly address saturated-salt humidity chambers after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, re-equilibration after disturbance, or air circulation in a desiccator. In the reported RH-XRD experiments, samples were initially equilibrated for 24 hours at relative humidities substantially below their expected equilibrium values. The humidity was then suddenly increased to a selected value above the expected equilibrium humidity, after which the humidity was maintained constant until the phase-transition reaction was complete. Reaction progress was monitored using successive X-ray diffraction measurements, generally one measurement every hour, with shorter 15-minute intervals in some experiments to improve time resolution. The apparatus used a humid-air generator that mixed dry and water-saturated air using automated mass-flow controllers, while temperature and humidity sensors near the sample provided feedback. Thus, the study demonstrates controlled forced air mixing and a 24-hour initial equilibration protocol, but gives no measured chamber recovery time following opening or disturbance and no comparison of fan versus no-fan conditions or desiccator circulation arrangements.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to equilibration and re-equilibration after a saturated-salt humidity chamber is opened or otherwise disturbed, but it does not provide a specific equilibration time, fan-speed recommendation, or direct comparison of stirred versus unstirred chambers. It emphasizes that salt–water systems may require relatively long periods to reach equilibrium because dissolution kinetics, ion diffusion, and moisture exchange with the surrounding environment all contribute. The time required for deliquescence increases as the imposed relative humidity approaches the salt solution’s equilibrium relative humidity, indicating especially slow adjustment near equilibrium. The authors describe equilibrium operationally through the absence of continuing sample-mass change: below the deliquescence point, water evaporates; above it, the mixture absorbs water; and equilibrium is reached when dm/dt equals zero. These observations support monitoring humidity and/or mass until the system stabilizes after exposure to ambient air. The passage does not discuss air circulation in a desiccator or the specific effect of a mixing fan, although environmental moisture exchange is identified as an important factor. It also warns that inadequate moisture control can produce RH calibration uncertainty as large as ±2.5%.

contexts.context: Greenspan’s study compiled 1,106 calculations from 21 investigations covering 89 saturated-salt solutions. It describes humidity determination by pressure comparison, calibrated sensors, and gravimetry (dry gas passed over solution, vapor absorbed and weighed). Relative humidity depends on temperature and vapor-pressure measurement method; errors vary with RH and temperature, so no method is universally best. Data were corrected for water-vapor pressure and air enhancement, then least-squares fitted as “RH = Σ Aᵢtⁱ” (typically cubic), with uncertainty estimates and temperature ranges reported for each salt.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. For tests (6) and (10): what does the literature report on (a) saturated-salt humidity chambers (Greenspan 1977; ISO 12571; OIML): accuracy, temperature sensitivity, equilibration time after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, sample size and layer thickness for gravimetric sorption, agreement with dynamic vapour sorption, and humidity effects on the flow of NaCl (deliquescence near 75 % RH), metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V) and pharmaceutical powders, including caking; (b) Faraday-cup measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio of powders after feeding, conveying or sieving: cup and shield design, electrometers versus home-built charge amplifiers (op-amp choice, feedback capacitor, leakage, guarding), collection efficiency for fines, typical charge-to-mass ratios for salts, metal powders and organic powders after contact with polymers (PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon) and steel, and their humidity dependence.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that saturated-salt RH values have publication-dependent uncertainty: sparse studies may yield misleadingly small standard deviations, so estimates used subjective components; generally, three standard deviations were adopted, with original-data uncertainty overriding fitted uncertainty when larger. Values are tabulated every 5°C, with extrapolation limited to 2.5°C. Reporting RH to 0.01% does **not** imply that accuracy; vapor-pressure and enhancement-equation uncertainties are excluded. For example, MgCl₂ equilibrium RH is approximately 33.5% at 10°C, 33.1% at 20°C, 32.4% at 30°C, and 31.6% at 40°C.

Reported uncertainties are typically ~0.1–0.7 percentage points, increasing at higher temperatures. Three differently weighted fits agreed within their assigned uncertainties. No Faraday-cup evidence appears in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance relevant to designing and evaluating an ADA4530-1 electrometer or charge-amplifier measurement system, particularly for very low-current and Faraday-cup charge measurements. It identifies electrometers as appropriate instruments because they have very high input impedance, low input bias current, minimal input voltage burden, and can resolve currents down to approximately 1 fA. The text emphasizes that leakage is a dominant error source in measurements below 1 pA. Guarding should surround the sensitive input trace with a driven guard maintained at the same or nearly the same potential, eliminating voltage differences that would cause leakage. A guarded PCB plane, via-fence, guarded cables/connectors, and careful pinout are also recommended. Moisture-resistant PCB materials, removal of solder mask around guard structures, and thorough cleaning are important because moisture and contamination can create leakage paths or electrolyte-like errors. Shielding the assembly in a grounded conductive enclosure reduces capacitive coupling and environmental interference. The excerpt does not specify ADA4530-1 parameters, feedback-capacitor selection, charge-amplifier transfer equations, or Faraday-cup geometry, so those aspects are not directly addressed.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general design guidance applicable to an ADA4530-1 electrometer/transimpedance charge amplifier for Faraday-cup measurements, although it does not mention the ADA4530-1 specifically. For pico-current circuitry, the op-amp should have very low input bias current, low voltage and current noise, and low offset drift; the comparison identifies CMOS as preferable, with a listed input-bias-current range of 0.1–10 pA. The amplifier and external input circuitry should be shielded, but shielding alone can introduce stray capacitance and leakage. A driven guard surrounding the input trace is recommended to reduce leakage and input capacitance; the guard should not be treated as ground, while grounded metallic shielding helps reject external interference. Input stray capacitance may be compensated with a capacitor placed in parallel with the feedback resistor. Because the capacitance is difficult to determine accurately, the feedback-capacitor value should be selected experimentally, and its effect on settling time and stability must be considered; smaller values are generally preferred. Leakage can also arise from dirty or moisture-absorbing PCBs, contamination, and poor insulation. Thorough cleaning with isopropyl alcohol or methanol and complete drying are recommended. For the lowest leakage and stray capacitance, the excerpt describes above-board turret-terminal wiring using high-resistivity insulating supports such as Teflon, though this is less suitable for commercial production.

contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. For tests (6) and (10): what does the literature report on (a) saturated-salt humidity chambers (Greenspan 1977; ISO 12571; OIML): accuracy, temperature sensitivity, equilibration time after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, sample size and layer thickness for gravimetric sorption, agreement with dynamic vapour sorption, and humidity effects on the flow of NaCl (deliquescence near 75 % RH), metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V) and pharmaceutical powders, including caking; (b) Faraday-cup measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio of powders after feeding, conveying or sieving: cup and shield design, electrometers versus home-built charge amplifiers (op-amp choice, feedback capacitor, leakage, guarding), collection efficiency for fines, typical charge-to-mass ratios for salts, metal powders and organic powders after contact with polymers (PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon) and steel, and their humidity dependence.

Question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. For tests (6) and (10): what does the literature report on (a) saturated-salt humidity chambers (Greenspan 1977; ISO 12571; OIML): accuracy, temperature sensitivity, equilibration time after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, sample size and layer thickness for gravimetric sorption, agreement with dynamic vapour sorption, and humidity effects on the flow of NaCl (deliquescence near 75 % RH), metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V) and pharmaceutical powders, including caking; (b) Faraday-cup measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio of powders after feeding, conveying or sieving: cup and shield design, electrometers versus home-built charge amplifiers (op-amp choice, feedback capacitor, leakage, guarding), collection efficiency for fines, typical charge-to-mass ratios for salts, metal powders and organic powders after contact with polymers (PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon) and steel, and their humidity dependence.

## Literature Review for Tests (6) and (10): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Faraday-Cup Charge-to-Mass Ratio Measurement

---

### Part (a): Saturated-Salt Humidity Chambers and Humidity Effects on Powder Flow

#### 1. Accuracy of Saturated-Salt Humidity Fixed Points

The definitive reference for saturated-salt humidity fixed points is Greenspan (1977), who compiled equilibrium relative humidity (RH) data for 28 binary saturated aqueous solutions using 1,106 measurements from 21 investigations, fitted as polynomial functions of temperature (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 1-2, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 2-3). Uncertainties were assigned as three times the standard deviation of the predicted values, with individual datum uncertainties propagated through a root-sum-square combination of contributions from temperature, pressure, equilibrium attainment, and sensor calibration (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 7-8, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 6-7). At 25 °C, the reported uncertainties for salts commonly used in humidity chambers are: LiCl 11.3 ± 0.3% RH; MgCl₂ 32.8 ± 0.2% RH; Mg(NO₃)₂ 52.9 ± 0.2% RH; NaCl 75.3 ± 0.2% RH; KCl 84.3 ± 0.3% RH; KNO₃ 93.6 ± 0.6% RH; and K₂SO₄ 97.3 ± 0.5% RH (lu2007uncertaintyevaluationof pages 1-2, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5). Lu and Chen (2007) used these Greenspan values to calibrate humidity sensors with vessels maintained at 25 ± 0.2 °C and 12-hour equilibration periods, reporting that the dominant contribution to combined uncertainty was the predicted calibration uncertainty of the sensor itself rather than the salt reference (lu2007uncertaintyevaluationof pages 1-2).

The following table summarizes the Greenspan fixed points for the specific salts proposed in the user's setup:

| Salt / humidity medium | RH at 25 °C (%) | Uncertainty (±% RH) | Approx. dRH/dT at 25 °C (% RH/°C) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| MgCl₂ | 32.78 | 0.16 | −0.06 | Saturated magnesium chloride fixed point; suitable for the low-RH chamber. (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5) |
| Mg(NO₃)₂ | 52.89 | 0.22 | −0.30 | Most temperature-sensitive listed salt point; a ±1 °C change shifts nominal RH by approximately ∓0.30 percentage points. (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5) |
| NaCl | 75.29 | 0.12 | −0.07 | Fixed point lies near NaCl’s deliquescence threshold; unsuitable for conditioning NaCl powder if it must remain safely below deliquescence. (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5) |
| KCl | 84.34 | 0.26 | −0.15 | High-RH fixed point; temperature control and condensation avoidance are especially important. (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4) |
| Silica gel | ≈0–5 | Not a Greenspan fixed-point uncertainty | Not applicable | Desiccant, not a saturated binary salt solution. RH depends on regeneration, loading, leakage, and sample moisture; verify it with the chamber sensor. |


*Table: Greenspan humidity fixed points and approximate temperature coefficients for the proposed salt chambers. Silica gel is included separately because it is a variable desiccant rather than a thermodynamic fixed point.*

#### 2. Temperature Sensitivity

The temperature coefficient dRH/dT varies considerably among salts. From the polynomial coefficients in Greenspan's Table 1 (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 2-3, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 3-4), NaCl has a relatively small temperature sensitivity of approximately −0.07% RH/°C near 25 °C, whereas Mg(NO₃)₂ is approximately −0.30% RH/°C—meaning that a ±1 °C temperature excursion shifts the nominal RH by ∓0.3 percentage points for Mg(NO₃)₂ but only ∓0.07 for NaCl. MgCl₂ has an even flatter coefficient (approximately −0.06% RH/°C), making it one of the most temperature-insensitive fixed points (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5). Rockland (1960) emphasized the desirability of salts with low temperature coefficients and warned that even small temperature variations can cause significant changes in equilibrium RH (rockland1960saturatedsaltsolutions pages 1-1). Rörig-Dalgaard and Svensson (2016) cautioned that heat of solution during salt dissolution or crystallization can locally change temperature and thus calibration RH, noting that inadequate moisture control can produce calibration uncertainty as large as ±2.5% RH (rorigdalgaard2016highaccuracycalibration pages 3-4).

#### 3. Equilibration Time and Effect of Mixing Fans

Equilibration time depends strongly on the salt, chamber volume, sample loading, and air circulation. In dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) calibration, salt-specific test durations ranged from approximately 6 hours for MgCl₂ to 20 hours for LiCl and KNO₃, with NaCl and Mg(NO₃)₂ requiring approximately 10 hours (rorigdalgaard2016highaccuracycalibration pages 6-8). For static desiccator-type chambers, equilibration can require days to weeks, particularly at high RH (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 1-5, imre1964themeasurementof pages 1-4). Rockland (1960) explicitly evaluated the effect of mechanical convection (a mixing fan) on equilibration rates and reported that fans decreased the time to achieve equilibration by 10 to 50 times compared to still-air conditions (rockland1960saturatedsaltsolutions pages 1-1). This strongly supports including a small circulating fan within each humidity chamber to accelerate recovery after opening.

#### 4. Sample Size and Layer Thickness for Gravimetric Sorption

Traditional saturated-salt-solution (SSS) gravimetric sorption methods typically require large samples of 10–100 g, with equilibration periods of days to weeks (burnettUnknownyearmoisturesorptionproperties pages 1-2). Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) instruments use much smaller samples, typically 20–100 mg, with equilibration at each RH step achievable in hours rather than days (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 5-9, munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 3-5). For the proposed few-gram setup using the doser, intermediate between these extremes, the key consideration is ensuring that the powder layer is thin enough for vapor to penetrate the bed rapidly. Arlabosse et al. (2003) found that for materials with apparent diffusion coefficients above approximately 10⁻⁹ m²/s, good agreement between static and dynamic methods was obtained; a 500 µm powder slab of microcrystalline cellulose gave diffusion coefficients of 1.7–4.4 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s and produced consistent results (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13, arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 5-9).

#### 5. Agreement Between DVS and Saturated-Salt Methods

Good agreement between DVS and SSS methods has been reported for several powder materials, particularly at low to intermediate RH. For microcrystalline cellulose, pharmaceutical granules, and barley straw, DVS and SSS isotherms generally agreed well (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13, bui2017comparisonofthe pages 6-9, bui2017comparisonofthe pages 1-6). Disagreement can arise at high water activity (above ~0.6–0.8) where slow internal diffusion limits the sample's ability to reach thermodynamic equilibrium within DVS step times (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13). The DVS mass-stability criterion is typically 100 times less stringent than the SSS criterion, which partly accounts for DVS being faster but potentially less accurate at high RH (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 5-9). For materials with dense or laminated structures, the methods may disagree because DVS results become dependent on sorption rate rather than thermodynamic equilibrium (schmidt2012comparisonbetweenwater pages 1-4).

#### 6. Humidity Effects on NaCl (Deliquescence Near 75% RH)

Sodium chloride has a deliquescence relative humidity (DRH) of approximately 75–76% at 25 °C (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33). Below this threshold, the crystalline phase is thermodynamically stable; at or above DRH, water uptake initiates dissolution and formation of a saturated aqueous solution. The dissolution rate is proportional to the difference between imposed RH and DRH (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 3-4). At 80% RH, approximately 25.5% of NaCl dissolves after four days; at 85% RH, 57.3%; and at 90% RH, 80.3% (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 6-9). Operating at exactly 75% RH places NaCl dangerously close to its DRH: small temperature or humidity fluctuations can trigger partial dissolution, formation of liquid bridges at particle contacts, and subsequent recrystallization upon drying, producing solid bridges and irreversible caking (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33). Dense NaCl powder aggregates can take days or weeks to deliquesce completely because vapor transport is restricted within the powder bed (linnow2006investigationofsodium pages 58-61, linnow2006investigationofsodium pages 54-58). This suggests that the NaCl chamber should ideally be omitted for conditioning NaCl powder itself, as the equilibrium RH of saturated NaCl coincides with NaCl's own DRH.

#### 7. Humidity Effects on Metal AM Powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V)

Among metal AM powders, AlSi10Mg is the most susceptible to moisture uptake, with moisture content increasing up to six times the initial value after conditioning at 50 °C and 80% RH for 72 hours (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 1-2). The irregular and rough particle morphology of AlSi10Mg promotes moisture adsorption through both physisorption and chemisorption, leading to thicker oxide layers, agglomeration via capillary bridges, and severely degraded spreadability (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 2-3). DVS measurements on similar AlSi7Mg powders showed that fine particles contribute most to moisture sorption due to their greater specific surface area; removing fines by sieving substantially reduced vapor uptake (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 5-8). Ti-6Al-4V, with its spherical and homogeneous particle morphology, shows very low moisture pickup in all tested states, indicating much lower sorption susceptibility (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 4-5). Nevertheless, even Ti-6Al-4V can form moisture-mediated agglomerates via capillary bridges (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11). Drying practices in the literature typically use 80–190 °C, with vacuum drying at 85 °C for 12 hours producing effective moisture removal (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 4-5, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 2-3).

#### 8. Humidity Effects on Pharmaceutical Powders and Caking

Pharmaceutical powders such as lactose are particularly susceptible to humidity-induced caking. Amorphous fractions within otherwise crystalline powders are hygroscopic and can crystallize when exposed to humid air, releasing water and forming solid bridges (afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 39-43). The caking mechanism involves condensation, dissolution, and recrystallization at particle contacts, driven by the difference between ambient RH and the material's critical RH or DRH (afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33, afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 39-43). Caking strength correlates with the rate and extent of crystallization, and repeated humidity cycling generally worsens the effect. Storage of hygroscopic powders over saturated solutions of MgCl₂, NaBr, NaCl, and KCl has been used to study caking at controlled RH levels (afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33).

### Part (b): Faraday-Cup Measurement of Powder Charge-to-Mass Ratio

#### 1. Cup and Shield Design

The standard Faraday cup for powder charge measurement consists of a conducting inner measurement cup surrounded by a larger grounded conducting outer cup, with an electrically insulating material (typically Teflon) separating them (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7, sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114, cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51). The outer cup functions as a Faraday cage, reducing electromagnetic background noise (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51, sowinski2012thestudyof pages 56-59). A BNC or coaxial cable connects the assembly to the measurement electronics: the cable shield connects to the grounded outer cup, while the center conductor connects to the inner cup (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51, cruise2023triboelectricchargingofb pages 47-51). Very high insulation between the inner and outer cups is required to minimize charge decay (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7). Sowinski (2012) described concentric cylindrical copper vessels with inner dimensions of 0.15 m diameter × 0.25 m height and outer dimensions of 0.20 m diameter × 0.33 m height, isolated by Teflon bolts and connected to a Keithley 6514 electrometer (sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114). For the proposed bench-top setup with a 3 mm doser outlet, a smaller aluminium cup inside a grounded can is appropriate.

#### 2. Collection Efficiency for Fines

Collection efficiency for fine particles is a recognized challenge. Sowinski (2012) used a reusable filter bag with only 26–30% capture efficiency for 1 µm particulates (sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114). Sun et al. (2019) designed a mini-Faraday cup with an internal metal disc filter specifically to achieve high collection efficiency for charged ultrafine particles in the 50–300 nm range, with measured current showing good linearity with particle concentration (sun2019designandevaluation pages 6-7). For the proposed setup collecting auger-dosed powder, ensuring that all fine particles land in the cup rather than being lost to air currents or electrostatic adhesion to walls is important; a deep cup geometry and controlled drop height help maximize collection.

#### 3. Electrometers Versus Home-Built Charge Amplifiers

Commercial electrometers (e.g., Keithley 6514) provide turnkey charge/current measurement with proven specifications but at high cost (sowinski2012thestudyof pages 108-114). For a home-built charge amplifier, the critical component is an electrometer-grade CMOS op-amp with ultra-low input bias current (mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 4-6, mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 1-2). Two leading candidates are:

- **LMP7721** (Texas Instruments): 3 fA typical input bias current, 17 MHz gain-bandwidth product, rail-to-rail output. Its ultra-low bias current makes it suitable for sub-picoampere transimpedance and charge-integrator circuits (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 17-20, currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 22-25).
- **ADA4530-1** (Analog Devices): ~20 fA typical input bias current, designed specifically for electrometer applications with on-chip guarding (sharmaUnknownyearabootstrappedesd pages 51-57).

The charge amplifier operates as an integrator: a known feedback capacitor C_F between the output and inverting input converts input charge to voltage according to q = C_F × V_F (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51). The feedback capacitor value determines both sensitivity and dynamic range; smaller capacitors give higher sensitivity but saturate sooner. A parallel high-value resistor or periodic reset switch prevents drift from integrating bias current (mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 1-2). Input capacitance (~11 pF for LMP7721) combined with PCB stray capacitance forms a pole with feedback components that can cause instability; a feedback capacitor may be needed for compensation, with the value determined experimentally (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 17-20).

#### 4. Leakage, Guarding, and Practical Implementation

At femtoampere current levels, leakage from PCB traces, connectors, and insulation dominates measurement error (sharmaUnknownyearabootstrappedesd pages 51-57). Guarding is essential: a driven guard trace surrounds the high-impedance input and feedback nodes, maintained at approximately the same potential as the protected node, so that voltage differences across insulation are eliminated and leakage current is diverted into the low-impedance guard rather than the input (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22, mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 4-6). The guard should form a complete conductive enclosure including guard planes connected through vias, with an external ground plane or shield protecting it from noise and leakage (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22). Triaxial cables extend guarding along cables to the Faraday cup (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22). Cleanliness is critical for sub-picoamp performance: flux residues, moisture, solvents, and contamination degrade leakage performance; PCB materials with low moisture absorption should be selected, and solder mask should be removed around guard structures (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22, sharmaUnknownyearabootstrappedesd pages 51-57). Teflon is the preferred insulating material for ultra-low-leakage applications (mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 4-6). Supply filtering with a low-noise linear regulator, ~100 Ω series resistance, and ≥100 µF bypass capacitor is recommended to prevent supply noise from coupling through ESD capacitance (~0.5 pF) at each input (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 22-25).

#### 6. Triboelectric Series Considerations for the PLA Auger

In the conventional triboelectric series, nylon is positioned on the strongly positive side, while PTFE (Teflon) is at the most negative extreme; polyethylene, polypropylene, and PVC occupy intermediate negative positions (peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 2-4, prawatya2018multivariateoptimisationand pages 21-24). PLA, though not always explicitly listed in older triboelectric series, has been shown experimentally to charge polymers either positively or sign-reverse relative to stainless steel: ABS charged negatively against stainless steel but positively against PLA, while PE and PP charged negatively against both (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5). This sign reversal demonstrates that the PLA auger tube will produce different charging polarities than a stainless-steel auger for the same powder, which is directly measurable with the proposed Faraday cup.

#### 7. Humidity Dependence of Triboelectric Charging

Humidity has a profound effect on triboelectric charging through multiple mechanisms: (i) adsorbed water layers increase surface conductivity, enabling charge dissipation; (ii) water bridges between contacting surfaces facilitate ion-mediated charge transfer; (iii) the dielectric strength of humid air is reduced, lowering the saturation charge on particles (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 100-104, sutka2023engineeringpolymerinterfaces pages 5-5). Experimentally, Dani et al. (2024) found that humid conditioning (96 hours at 82% RH) reduced the absolute charge-to-mass ratio to approximately 50–70% of normal values across all tested polymers (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5). Schella et al. (2017) demonstrated that polymer granulates became highly charged at low humidity (<30% RH) but acquired almost no charge above 80% RH, with the transition RH depending on the material (sutka2023engineeringpolymerinterfaces pages 5-5). For polymer contacts, charging was found to reach a maximum near 30% RH and decrease above 40% RH (sutka2023engineeringpolymerinterfaces pages 5-5). Bailey (1993) reported that for polyethylene, dry conditions produced bipolar charging (coarse positive, fines negative), while high humidity caused all particles to charge negatively; at ~35% RH, net charge was approximately zero (bailey1993chargingofsolids pages 6-9). These findings indicate that the Faraday cup measurements should be performed at controlled and recorded humidity, ideally pairing them with the humidity chambers from test (6) to systematically map the charge–humidity relationship for each powder.
