### Summary and Practical Recommendations

For **test (6)**, the saturated-salt humidity chambers provide thermodynamic fixed points with Greenspan-tabulated uncertainties of ±0.1–0.5% RH at 25 °C (lu2007uncertaintyevaluationof pages 1-2, greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5). Temperature control to ±0.5 °C is advisable, particularly for Mg(NO₃)₂ whose dRH/dT is approximately −0.3% RH/°C (greenspan1977humidityfixedpoints pages 4-5). Including a small circulating fan reduces equilibration time by 10–50× (rockland1960saturatedsaltsolutions pages 1-1). After opening a chamber to load or remove a sample, re-equilibration with fan assistance should be verified by monitoring the SHT45 sensor until readings stabilize to within ±0.5% RH. For gravimetric sorption on a few grams of powder, thin layers (< ~1 mm) on the balance pan will help ensure that vapor diffusion is not rate-limiting, as agreement with DVS is good when bed diffusivity exceeds ~10⁻⁹ m²/s (arlabosse2003comparisonbetweenstatic pages 9-13). NaCl powder should not be conditioned at the NaCl-saturated chamber (~75% RH) because this coincides with its own DRH, risking irreversible caking (langlet2011kineticsofdissolution pages 1-3, afrassiabian2019multiscaleinvestigationof pages 29-33). AlSi10Mg is the most moisture-sensitive of the metal AM powders and should be prioritized for humidity-dosing characterization (cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 10-11, cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 1-2).

For **test (10)**, the Faraday cup should use a deep aluminium inner cup inside a grounded can, connected to a femtoampere-grade charge amplifier via guarded cabling (cruise2023triboelectricchargingof pages 47-51, currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22). The LMP7721 (3 fA bias) or ADA4530-1 (~20 fA bias) are suitable op-amps for a home-built integrating charge amplifier, with feedback capacitor values chosen to match the expected charge range of ~0.1–100 nC per dose (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 17-20, currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 22-25). Driven guard traces, Teflon insulation, triaxial cables, and meticulous cleanliness are essential for meaningful sub-picoampere measurements (currentUnknownyearlmp77213femtoampereinput pages 20-22, mortuza2017picocurrentmeasurementchallenges pages 4-6). Expected charge-to-mass ratios from auger feeding through a PLA tube are likely in the 1–10 nC/g range for most powders, with significant humidity dependence (dani2024effectofmoisture pages 4-5, bailey1993chargingofsolids pages 6-9). Pairing Faraday-cup measurements before and after humidity conditioning will provide a direct link between tests (6) and (10).

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A 25 mm OD tube with a 21 mm bore and a helical flight ends in a 3 mm outlet; a NEMA 11 stepper turns it at 1-109 rpm, servos tilt it 0-90 degrees, a solenoid taps it, and doses fall onto a 0.1 mg analytical balance. We record a dosing fingerprint (mass per revolution vs tilt and speed, mass per tap, afterflow, no-flow fraction) on 13 powders (NaCl, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, silicon, rice flours, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 dihydrate, fumed silica and others) and calibrate a LIGGGHTS DEM twin. Property labels from handbooks limit our models (angle-of-repose ranges 6-16 degrees wide), so we are designing ten small in-house tests built around the doser, each using a few grams and run on the same jar and day as the fingerprint: (1) heap angle of repose on a 20 mm fixed pedestal on the balance, photographed in silhouette; (2) bulk and tapped density in a 10 mL Class A cylinder filled by the auger and tapped by a cam drop of 3 mm at 250 taps/min, column height read by camera; (3) a servo tilting plate with an IMU: wall friction of a 25 mm powder-filled ring at 70-450 Pa on PLA, stainless steel and glass, and the start angle of 1-5 mm powder layers; (4) particle size and shape from backlit images with a Raspberry Pi HQ camera and a 0.12-1.8x zoom lens; (5) a 25 mm cup with 1-6 mm orifice discs and a servo gate emptying onto the balance (Beverloo fit, smallest orifice that flows, with and without taps); (6) humidity chambers held by saturated salt solutions (MgCl2, Mg(NO3)2, NaCl, KCl, silica gel) with SHT45 sensors, weighing uptake and dosing before and after; (7) a 40 mm by 15 mm rotating drum driven by the doser's stepper, 1-20 rpm; (8) unconfined yield strength of a 20 mm by 40 mm column from a split mould after 0.2-2 kPa consolidation, crushed by a lead-screw platen on a 100 g load cell; (9) a blade spreading a 0.1-0.2 mm layer over a 100 x 30 mm coupon at 10-100 mm/s; (10) a Faraday cup (aluminium cup in a grounded can) with a femtoamp op-amp charge amplifier under the doser outlet. For tests (6) and (10): what does the literature report on (a) saturated-salt humidity chambers (Greenspan 1977; ISO 12571; OIML): accuracy, temperature sensitivity, equilibration time after opening, the effect of a mixing fan, sample size and layer thickness for gravimetric sorption, agreement with dynamic vapour sorption, and humidity effects on the flow of NaCl (deliquescence near 75 % RH), metal AM powders (AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V) and pharmaceutical powders, including caking; (b) Faraday-cup measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio of powders after feeding, conveying or sieving: cup and shield design, electrometers versus home-built charge amplifiers (op-amp choice, feedback capacitor, leakage, guarding), collection efficiency for fines, typical charge-to-mass ratios for salts, metal powders and organic powders after contact with polymers (PLA, PTFE, PETG, nylon) and steel, and their humidity dependence.
